fields.title: The Third Epoch In My Religious Life (the Restitution Of All Things)
fields.body_html:
As I stated in the last chapter, after a few years of exuberant joy in the good news of salvation through Christ — for myself and for those who believed as I did — my heart began reaching outward toward those who believed differently, and especially toward those who, through the providential circumstances of their birth and surroundings, had never had a fair chance in life. I could not help seeing that ignorance of God, and therefore lives of sin, seemed the almost inevitable fate of vast numbers of my fellow human beings. And I could not reconcile it with the justice of God that such unfortunate souls should be doomed to eternal torment for circumstances for which they were not responsible and from which, in the great majority of cases, they could not escape.

The fact that I, who no more deserved it than they, had been brought to the knowledge of the truth while they were left out in the cold became so burdensome to me that I often felt I would gladly give up my own salvation if, by that means, I could bestow it upon those placed in less fortunate conditions than my own.

I began to feel that the salvation in which I had rejoiced was, after all, a narrow and selfish salvation —unworthy of the Creator who has so emphatically declared that His “tender mercies are over all His works,” and even more unworthy of the Lord Jesus Christ, who came into the world for the single purpose of saving the world. I could not believe that His life and death for us were intended to fall so far short of remedying the very evil He came expressly to remedy. I felt it must be impossible that there could be any shortcoming in the salvation He had provided.

I became convinced that my difficulties had arisen simply from misunderstanding God’s plans, and I set myself earnestly to discover my mistake. As I have said, my first refuge had been the annihilation of the wicked. But this soon seemed unworthy of a wise and good Creator — indeed, a sad confession of failure on His part — and I could not reconcile it with His omnipotence or His omniscience. I began to fear I was going to be disappointed in God.

But one day a revelation came that vindicated Him and settled the whole question forever.

We often had revivalist preachers staying in our home, as we sought every opportunity to help forward what we called “gospel work.” Among them came one who was very much taken up with the idea that it was the privilege and duty of Christians to share, in a special manner, in the sufferings of Christ as well as in His joys. He seemed to think that doing so would somehow help those who knew nothing of salvation in Christ; and he had adopted the practice of making strong appeals on this subject in his meetings. He would ask Christians who were willing, for the sake of others, to take a share of Christ’s sufferings upon themselves, to “come forward” to a front bench in the meeting and pray that such a privilege might be granted them.

Somehow it all sounded very grand and heroic, and it fit so exactly with my own longings to help my less fortunate fellow human beings that, although I did not go forward for prayer at any of his meetings, I did begin privately to pray — blindly and ignorantly — that I might come into the experience, whatever it was.

The result was very different from what I had expected, and far more tremendous.

I had expected to enter into a sense of Christ’s personal sufferings in the life and death He bore for our sakes. Instead, I seemed to receive a revelation, not of His sufferings because of sin, but of ours . I seemed to see the misery and anguish brought upon humanity by the entrance of sin into the world, and Christ’s sorrow— not over His own suffering because of it, but over the suffering of the poor human beings who had been cursed by it.

I seemed to understand something of what His anguish must be at the sight of the awful fate permitted to befall the human race, and of His joy that He could do something to alleviate it. I saw that ours was the suffering, and His was the joy of sacrificing Himself to save us. I felt that if I had been a Divine Creator and had allowed such a dreadful fate to overtake the creatures I had made, I would have been filled with anguish and would have realized that simple justice — even if not love — required that I find some remedy for it. And I knew I could not be more just than God.

Over and over, I found myself repeating in my heart the lines that George MacDonald places on a tombstone in one of his stories: “Oh Thou who didst the serpent make, Our pardon give, and pardon take.”

I had heard a great deal about the awfulness of our sins against God; but now I found myself asking: What about the awfulness of our fate in having been made sinners? Would I not infinitely rather that someone commit a sin against me than that I commit a sin against anyone else? Was it not far more dreadful to be made a sinner than to be sinned against?

And I began to see that, since God had permitted sin to enter the world, it must necessarily follow that, in common fairness, He would be compelled to provide a remedy equal to the disease. I remembered mothers I had known whose children suffered from inherited diseases, and who were only too thankful to lay down their lives in self-sacrifice if, in any way, they could undo the harm they had caused by bringing these children into the world under such disastrous conditions. And I asked myself: Could God do less?

I saw that when weighed on the balance of wrong endured, we , who had been created sinners, had infinitely more to forgive than anyone against whom we ourselves may have sinned.

The vividness with which all this came to me can never be expressed. I did not think it, or imagine it, or suppose it. I saw it. It was a revelation of the real nature of things — not according to surface, conventional ideas, but according to the actual underlying facts — and it could not be denied. In every human face I saw, there seemed to be unveiled before me the story of the misery and anguish that had entered the world through sin. I knew that God must see this with far clearer eyes than mine, and therefore His suffering from the sight must be infinitely greater — even though mine already felt nearly unbearable. And I began to understand how the least He could do would be to embrace with untold gladness anything that would help to deliver the beings He had created from such awful misery.

It was an unforgettable insight into the world’s anguish because of sin.

How long it lasted I cannot remember, but while it did, it nearly crushed me. And because it always returned at the sight of a stranger’s face, I found myself forced to wear a thick veil whenever I went out into the streets, so that I might spare myself the terrible impact of that realization.

One day I was riding on a tram-car along Market Street in Philadelphia when two men came in and sat opposite me. I saw them dimly through my veil and felt relieved — dimness meant protection. When the conductor came for my fare, I had to lift the veil to count out the coins. As I raised it, I caught a full view of those two faces, and an overwhelming flood of anguish swept through me. I seemed to receive yet another revelation — clearer and deeper — of the misery sin had brought upon humanity. It was more than I could bear. I clenched my hands and cried out inwardly, “Oh God, how can You endure it? You might have prevented it, but did not. You might even now change it, but You do not. I do not see how You can continue to live and endure such a sight.”

I upbraided God. And I felt justified in doing so.

Then, suddenly, God seemed to answer me. An inward voice spoke in tones of infinite love and tenderness: “He shall see of the travail of His soul, and be satisfied.”

“Satisfied!” I cried within myself. “Christ is to be satisfied! He will look upon the world’s misery, and then upon the travail He has endured because of it, and He will be satisfied with the result! If I were Christ, nothing could satisfy me unless every human being were ultimately saved. Therefore, nothing less can satisfy Him.”

With that, a veil seemed to be lifted from the plans of the universe. I saw that it was true, as the Bible declares, that “As in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.” As was the first, so was the second. The “all” in one case could not fairly mean anything less than the “all” in the other. I saw, therefore, that the remedy must be equal to the disease — that salvation must be as universal as the fall.

I saw all this that day on the tram-car on Market Street — not merely thought it, or hoped it, or believed it, but knew it. It was a Divine fact. And from that moment, I have never had a doubt about the final destiny of the human race. God is the Creator of every human being; therefore He is the Father of each one, and they are all His children. And Christ died for every one, declared to be the “propitiation not for our sins only, but also for the sins of the whole world” (1 John 2:2).

However great the ignorance, however grievous the sin, the promise of salvation is absolute and without limitation.

If it is true that “by the offense of one judgment came upon all men to condemnation,” then it is equally true that “by the righteousness of one the free gift came upon all men unto justification of life.” To limit the latter “all men” is also to limit the former. The salvation is exactly equal to the fall. There is to be a final “restitution of all things,” when “at the name of Jesus every knee shall bow — of things in heaven, and things on earth, and things under the earth — and every tongue shall confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” Every knee, every tongue — nothing could be more all-embracing.

The how and the when I could not see. But the essential fact was all I needed: somewhere, somehow, God was going to make everything right for all the creatures He had made. My heart rested in this forever.

I hurried home eager to reach my Bible, to see whether this magnificent truth I had discovered could possibly have been there all along without my noticing it. The moment I entered the house, I did not even remove my bonnet, but rushed to the table where my Bible and Concordance always lay ready. I began to search — and instantly the whole Book seemed illuminated. On every page the truth about the “times of restitution of all things,” of which the Apostle Peter says “God hath spoken by the mouth of all His holy prophets since the world began,” shone forth, leaving no room for doubt.

I turned eagerly from page to page, laughing aloud for joy at the blaze of light that filled it. It became a new book. It was as though another skin had been peeled off every text, and each verse shone with new meaning — not a different meaning, for the new did not contradict the old, but a deeper meaning, the true meaning hidden within the outward form of words. Nothing in the text needed changing; only my understanding needed to be opened. And now, at last, it was.

I remember soon afterward, in the course of my daily Bible reading, coming to the Psalms and being astonished at the new light thrown upon their most severe — even seemingly bloodthirsty — denunciations. I saw that, when read in the spirit rather than the letter, they were full of the promised and final triumph of good over evil, and were a magnificent vindication of the goodness and justice of God, who will not — and ought not, and cannot — rest until all His enemies, and ours, are placed beneath His feet.

I saw that His kingdom must be inward before it can be outward; that it is a kingdom of ideas, not of brute force; that His rule is over hearts, not over territories; that His victories must occur within before they are visible without. He seeks to rule spirits rather than bodies. No victory could satisfy Him except the victory that wins the heart — the surrender of the free and convinced soul, not the mere capitulation of the conquered slave. As Milton says, “Who overcomes by force hath overcome but half his foe,” and I saw this was true.

Read in this light, the very words that had once filled me with horror now thrilled my soul with praise: “Let God arise, let His enemies be scattered; let them also that hate Him flee before Him.

As smoke is driven away, so drive them away; as wax melts before the fire, so let the wicked perish at the presence of God.”

God’s wrath is against sin , not the sinner; and when His enemies are scattered, ours are scattered with them. His sword is righteousness, which puts sin to death so that the sinner may live. The fire of His anger is the refiner’s fire ; He sits not as the destroyer of the soul but as its purifier, to cleanse it as gold and silver are purified.

“Implacable is love.

Foes may be bought or teased From their malign intent; But He goes unappeased Who is on kindness bent.”

The Psalmist says, “Thou wast a God that forgavest them, though thou tookest vengeance of their inventions”; and with this key in hand, all the denunciations of God’s wrath— once so cruel and unjust to my ears — were transformed into declarations of His loving determination to make us good enough to live with Him in Heaven forever.

I could multiply examples endlessly of this new illumination that shone in entrancing beauty across every page of Scripture, but these are enough. At last I began to understand what the Apostle Paul meant when he said he had been made a minister of the new covenant, “not of the letter, but of the spirit; for the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.” The things I had once read in the letter and shuddered at, now — read in the spirit — filled me with joy.

It was as though another skin had been peeled off every text, and each verse shone with new meaning — not a different meaning, for the new did not contradict the old, but a deeper meaning, the true meaning hidden within the outward form of words. Nothing in the text needed changing; only my understanding needed to be opened. And now, at last, it was. I remember soon afterward, in the course of my daily Bible reading, coming to the Psalms and being astonished at the new light thrown upon their most severe — even seemingly bloodthirsty — denunciations. I saw that, when read in the spirit rather than the letter, they were full of the promised and final triumph of good over evil, and were a magnificent vindication of the goodness and justice of God, who will not — and ought not, and cannot — rest until all His enemies, and ours, are placed beneath His feet. I saw that His kingdom must be inward before it can be outward; that it is a kingdom of ideas, not of brute force; that His rule is over hearts, not over territories; that His victories must occur within before they are visible without. He seeks to rule spirits rather than bodies. No victory could satisfy Him except the victory that wins the heart — the surrender of the free and convinced soul, not the mere capitulation of the conquered slave. As Milton says, “Who overcomes by force hath overcome but half his foe,” and I saw this was true. Read in this light, the very words that had once filled me with horror now thrilled my soul with praise: “Let God arise, let His enemies be scattered; let them also that hate Him flee before Him. As smoke is driven away, so drive them away; as wax melts before the fire, so let the wicked perish at the presence of God.” God’s wrath is against sin , not the sinner; and when His enemies are scattered, ours are scattered with them. His sword is righteousness, which puts sin to death so that the sinner may live. The fire of His anger is the refiner’s fire ; He sits not as the destroyer of the soul but as its purifier, to cleanse it as gold and silver are purified. “Implacable is love. Foes may be bought or teased From their malign intent; But He goes unappeased Who is on kindness bent.” The Psalmist says, “Thou wast a God that forgavest them, though thou tookest vengeance of their inventions”; and with this key in hand, all the denunciations of God’s wrath— once so cruel and unjust to my ears — were transformed into declarations of His loving determination to make us good enough to live with Him in Heaven forever. I could multiply examples endlessly of this new illumination that shone in entrancing beauty across every page of Scripture, but these are enough. At last I began to understand what the Apostle Paul meant when he said he had been made a minister of the new covenant, “not of the letter, but of the spirit; for the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.” The things I had once read in the letter and shuddered at, now — read in the spirit — filled me with joy.

fields.title: The Unselfishness Of God
fields.body_html:
I have always felt that this was the moment when I truly discovered the unselfishness of God .

Until then, although I rejoiced in the salvation I had found for myself, I still suffered from a secret, torturing suspicion that, in the end, it was a rather selfish salvation —both on God’s part and on mine.

How could a good God enjoy Himself in Heaven while knowing that a large proportion of the beings He Himself had created were doomed to eternal misery — unless He were, in some way, a selfish God? I knew the Bible said He was a God of love, and I supposed it must be true. But deep down there remained that hidden feeling that His love could not stand comparison with the ideal of love I felt in my own heart.

I knew that, imperfect as my love was, I could never enjoy Heaven while even one of my children — no matter how disobedient — was shut out. And the thought that God could , and did , enjoy Heaven while countless thousands of His children were shut out seemed to reveal a failure in the most essential element of love. So even while I was grateful for forgiveness and the sure hope of Heaven for myself, I often felt that the God I worshipped must be a selfish God, caring more for His own comfort and His glory than for the suffering beings He had made.

But now I began to see that the wideness of God’s love was far beyond anything I had ever imagined. If I gathered together all the unselfish love of every mother’s heart in the whole world, multiplied it by millions, and pressed it into one place, I would still have nothing more than a faint shadow of the unselfishness of God.

I had always thought of Him as loving. But now I discovered something far deeper: He did not merely possess love — He was love itself , love embodied and woven into the very essence of His being.

I saw that God was, as it were, made of love, so that in the very nature of things He could not act contrary to love. It wasn’t that He chose not to — it was that He could not , because love was the very essence of His nature. The law of love, like the law of gravity, is inevitable in its operation.

God, if I may say so, is under this law and cannot help obeying it. And once I understood this, trusting the God of love became as natural as breathing. Every doubt evaporated, and I was filled with boundless delight at the thought of having been created by such an unselfish God.

I saw that His role as Creator was, in itself, an absolute guarantee that He would care for us and make all things work together for our good. The responsibilities of ownership blazed with breathtaking clarity. Not the rights of ownership — as I had always thought — but its duties , the obligations that ownership imposes.

Just as, in a civilized society, people are held responsible — by public opinion or even by law — to care properly for the things they own, so our Creator is necessarily bound, by the moral law of His own nature, to take proper care of the beings He has made. He must be held responsible for our well-being.

It was all so glorious that it often seemed almost too good to be true — that we truly belonged to such an unselfish God. Many a time, when some new insight into His goodness overwhelmed me, I would take my Bible, open it to the passages declaring that we belong to Him, and put my fingers on the verses, reading them aloud just to reassure myself that they really did say — freely and without limitation — that He was indeed my Owner.

The phrase, “Remember thy Creator,” suddenly took on a wholly different character. I had always thought of it as a warning meant to frighten us into good behavior. Now it shone with comfort — a delightful assurance that everything must be well with the creatures of such an unselfish Creator.

I saw that God was good not merely in a religious sense, but in the truest, most practical sense of the word. And a good Creator was, of course, bound to make everything go right with His creation. The fact that nothing was hidden from His eyes — once so terrifying — became the most comforting truth in the universe, because it meant He knew all about us and could therefore do His best for us.

My own experience as a mother — once a source of conflict with my beliefs about God — now came into perfect harmony. My children have been the joy of my life. I cannot imagine bliss more exquisite than the moments when my arms have been around them. Those moments have seemed nearer to the joy of Heaven than anything else on earth. And I think this joy has taught me more about God’s feelings toward His children than anything else.

If I, a finite human being with limited capacity, could find such joy in my children, what must God — with His infinite heart — feel for His? Most of my understanding of the love of God has come from this very experience. I could not believe that God had created me with a greater capacity for unselfish love and self-sacrifice than He possessed Himself. Since discovering the mother-heart of God, I have answered every doubt about God ’s love simply by looking into my own heart as a mother.

To me, it is impossible that a true mother could be selfish toward her children. A mother who puts her own comfort and welfare before her children is, in my mind, an unnatural mother, one who has failed in her highest calling. And if one looks at what we call the lower creation, even the animals teach us the supreme duty of maternal self-giving. The mother tiger will die before she lets harm come to her young. She will starve so they may eat. Could God do less?

I speak of self-sacrifice, but in truth I cannot really call it sacrifice. No true mother — one who knows the reality of motherhood — would ever regard her care for her children as a sacrifice. It may involve exhaustion or hardship, but not sacrifice in the ordinary sense. The real sacrifice would be if she were not allowed to care for them.

For this reason, I believe that many disappointed mothers — who do not receive the gratitude they desire — have only themselves to blame, because they demanded gratitude rather than inspired it.

This understanding has revealed to me God’s feelings toward us: that what we call Christ’s “self-sacrifice” was simply the natural and necessary expression of His love; and that the astonishing thing is not that He did it, but that He could not have done otherwise .

Since discovering the mother-heart of God, I have never been able to feel the slightest anxiety for any of His children — and by His children, I do not mean only the good ones, but the bad ones equally. Did not Jesus tell us that the Good Shepherd leaves the ninety-nine safe sheep to search for the one that is lost, and does not rest until He finds it?

Viewed in the light of motherhood, the word “lost” becomes profoundly comforting. Nothing can be “lost” unless it is owned by someone. To be lost means only, “not yet found.” The lost coin is still gold, bearing the king’s image. The lost sheep is still a sheep, not a wolf. The lost son is still a son, with his father’s blood in his veins.

So if a person is a “lost sinner,” it simply means he is owned by the Good Shepherd, and that the Shepherd, by the very duties of ownership, must go after that which is lost — and keep going until He finds it.

To me, the word “lost” contains the strongest possible proof of ownership.

Who can imagine a mother with a lost child having one moment of rest until the child is found?

And who could imagine God being less concerned than a mother?

I believe that all the problems of the spiritual life , which so often distress conscientious souls, would disappear like morning mist before the rising sun if only the full blaze of the mother-heart of God were allowed to shine upon them.

I came to see that, since Scripture declares we were created in the image of God, we are obliged to believe that the best in us — not the worst — is what reflects that image. Anything that, in our highest and most unselfish moments, appears selfish, unkind, unjust, or self-seeking must never be attributed to God, no matter how things may “seem.” If God is unselfish, then He must be at least as unselfish as the noblest ideal we can conceive — and of course infinitely more.

All the biblical texts about God’s goodness suddenly shone with new meaning. I realized that His goodness is not a condescending benevolence but a genuine, wholehearted goodness — one that includes true unselfishness, deep consideration, and above all, justice. Justice has always seemed to me one of the first essentials of goodness; I cannot imagine calling anyone “good” who is unjust, no matter how impressive their outward appearance of virtue may be. In short, I had, such an overwhelming revelation of God’s intrinsic and inherent goodness and unselfishness that nothing since has been able to shake it. Many aspects of His dealings with the world have been,, and still are, mysterious to me; but I am convinced that every one of them could be explained through the lens of His love and justice, if only I could see deeply enough. And I believe that one day I will see clearly what I now hold by faith: that His loving kindness truly reaches over all His works.

I do not mean that all this understanding came to me at once. But I do mean that on that day, riding a tramcar in Philadelphia, a light broke across the character of God — a light that has never dimmed in the slightest and has only grown brighter with each passing year.

For me, it is enough to say, “God is,” and the answer to every difficulty is already present. What amazes me is that I, along with so many other Christians, had failed to see this, even with the open Bible before us —and that all sorts of distortions of God’s character, even outright slanders against His goodness, can find a ready welcome in Christian hearts. To me, such misrepresentations became almost unbearable. I could listen patiently — even with interest — to almost any strange or unorthodox idea that did not malign God’s character. But the one thing I could not endure, the one thing I could not sit quietly through, was anything that — even under a cloak of piety —suggested the faintest insult to God’s love or His unselfishness.

I will never forget a memorable incident in our home when a distinguished preacher from Boston was visiting us. At breakfast, the conversation turned to God’s love. He insisted that you must not rely on it too much, for there were limits to what God could endure — just as, he said, there were limits to a mother’s love. He claimed that a daughter might commit certain sins a mother could never forgive, sins that would forever close her heart and her home, and he argued that God was the same. To believe otherwise, he said, was to hold a “grandmotherly religion.”

I have no doubt he meant to undermine my views on Restitution, though we were not discussing that topic. He simply wished to convince me that God was not as “foolishly loving” as I believed. But to hear mothers, and the God who created mothers, so misrepresented was more than I could bear. Though he was my guest, I burst out in fierce indignation, declared that I would not sit at the table with anyone who held such slanderous ideas of God, and left the room in tears. I refused to see him again. I do not claim that this reaction was courteous or even Christ-like, but it shows how overwhelmingly I felt about the matter. To me, the honor of God outweighed every rule of social etiquette.

I see now that I might have defended that honor just as strongly, but in a far more Christ-like way. Still, to this day, the one thing I find extremely hard to tolerate is anything that maligns the character of God. Nothing else compares to this in importance, for our entire salvation depends absolutely on who God is. Unless he can be shown to be wholly good, wholly unselfish, and wholly just, then our case is utterly hopeless. God alone is our salvation, and if He fails us — even in the smallest degree — we have nowhere else to turn.

fields.title: Effect Of My Views On My Public Work
fields.body_html:
As could be expected in those days, my views on Restitution — views I announced rather quickly — met with considerable disapproval from the Plymouth Brethren and many of my other orthodox friends. I had to endure a fair amount of what might be called persecution, though in truth I took a certain satisfaction in it, for I felt it was a grand thing to know so much more of God than those who opposed me.

I often compared my feelings to those of a civilized traveler trying to explain the marvels of his world to people in a remote, “savage” country— people who could neither understand nor believe what he described. His sense of superior knowledge would make their disapproval and opposition only a reason to pity their ignorance and to bear with it patiently. On that same principle, I almost enjoyed being regarded as a heretic, and I never wanted anyone’s endorsement. To be endorsed felt, to me, like being bound; and I preferred to be a free lance, unhindered in my absolute mental and spiritual freedom.

At that time the discovery I had made was not as widely known as it is now, and it seemed likely that holding what many considered a grave heresy might hinder my Christian work. And perhaps it did in some circles. But as I always had far more invitations to speak than I could possibly accept, I never truly suffered any difficulty. I tried to be courteous enough not to place on others — especially those who found my views abhorrent — the burden of endorsing me. Still, the revelation I had received was too glorious to withhold whenever a door opened. And since I refused to sail under false colors, and insisted that any place I spoke should know beforehand exactly what a “heretic” I was, I generally enjoyed all the freedom I desired.

In fact, these very views — and my open confession of them under rather trying circumstances — opened the way for some of our most important and fruitful work. It happened in this way.

In 1873, my husband came to England to hold meetings in the interests of the Higher Life, or what I prefer to call the Life of Faith. I followed soon after, and upon my arrival in London I was invited to meet a gathering of leading Evangelical ladies who were to decide whether it would be safe for them to support me and lend their influence to the work.

Lady Mount Temple, one of the women present, later described the meeting in her life of Lord Mount Temple: “I think it was in 1873 that Mr. Pearsall Smith came to England from America, followed a few months later by his dear, beautiful wife. It was a time long to be remembered. They came, one may say, full of the new wine of the Spirit, longing to help others onward in the Divine life. A friend invited us to lunch to meet them. I shall never forget my first sight of Hannah Smith. We called her the ‘angel of the Churches,’ and she looked like one, with her golden hair and clear, beautifully cut face, in a dress all her own, yet as simple as that of the Friends among whom she had been raised.

“What especially drew me to her that day was this. I must confess that I was only a seeker after truth. Hannah was sitting in a small circle of excellent orthodox friends, gathered to hear the good things she had to share, and she was, in fact, on trial. She had seen a funeral procession in the street, and when she mentioned it, we all adopted the conventional expression of sorrow.

‘Oh,’ she said, ‘when I see a funeral I always give thanks for a brother or sister delivered from the trials and pains of this mortal state.’ I thought, How wonderful! And I could not help asking, ‘Is that possible? Do you feel this about everyone?’ I was indeed an enfant terrible.

“She paused for a moment and glanced around. She was among evangelicals, at a time when the universal hope was considered a heresy, and this was her examination. She later said she experienced a brief inner struggle. But truth prevailed, and with her bright, fearless look she said, ‘Yes— about everyone. For I trust in the love of God.’ I surrendered my heart immediately to this trust, love, and candor.”

I remember the occasion perfectly, and the thoughts running through my mind. I knew I was being tested, and I suspected that my answer might shock the entire company. But I felt that loyalty to God required me to say what honored Him, and to leave the consequences in His hands.

The moment I finished speaking, Lady Mount Temple — then Mrs. Cowper Temple — rose from her seat, came straight to me, and, though I was a stranger, gave me a warm, affectionate kiss.

“You must come and hold some meetings at Broadlands,” she said at once. I don’t know what the others felt, but not a word of disapproval was spoken, and they later became some of my dearest friends.

The result was that, within a few weeks, Broadlands — the country home of Lord and Lady Mount Temple in Hampshire — was opened to us for our first conference. It was a time of extraordinary blessing, and it became the doorway to all the later conferences and to our entire subsequent work in England and beyond.

When a conference was planned at Brighton in 1874, some members of the organizing committee became anxious about my “heresies,” fearing they might hinder the work. They persuaded my husband — who had arrived in England before I did — to write to me in America and tell me that unless I promised to keep my views quiet, they would strongly oppose my participation in the meetings. Recently, while looking through an old bundle of letters, I found my reply, which reveals precisely how I felt at the time: “Philadelphia, April 6, 1874.

Thy letters from London have arrived. Thee need not think I would be troubled at not being allowed to speak in the meetings, for nothing would suit me better. I am not in the least anxious to preach. Indeed, I consider it quite a favor on my part to be willing to do it at all, and just as much of a favor on others’ part to listen to me. If your committee should say, ‘We do not want to hear you speak at Brighton,’ I would have thanked them heartily. No one need feel any delicacy about this. But it must be thoroughly understood that I will make no compromises for anyone, and that I believe in Restitution more firmly than ever. I do not think I could bear the misery I see in this poor, sad, sin-stricken world without it. Our temperance work brings us face to face with such helpless suffering that my heart would break if I did not know that God loves all His creatures and has something gracious in store for everyone.”

Since I would not compromise — and since it was still considered important to have me at the meetings — the committee dropped the matter and decided to take me as I was, heresies and all.

When my husband wrote to tell me this, I replied: “Philadelphia.

I am very glad thee has escaped thy difficulty about thy heretical preaching wife with so little trouble. But the idea of B — , with his shaky views, undertaking to excommunicate me! I do not think it honest. I will not sail under false colors, and my conviction about Restitution grows stronger every single day. If they leave me alone in England, I will probably say little about it; but if there is even the slightest hint of compromise or secrecy on my part, I will blaze out into a perfect conflagration. I cannot endure anything of that sort. So please remember this, ye Lords of Creation.

Seriously, though, I do not feel drawn to preach or teach Restitution over there, and if the dear, frightened orthodox friends make no fuss about it, I am unlikely to do so. Their worries about me do not annoy me in the least. I believe I actually enjoy being the target of the odium theologicum.

I suppose there is something of the war horse in my constitution.”

Whether the committee’s fears were well founded or not, I cannot say; I only know that not once, during all my work in England, did I ever feel that my views on Restitution hindered the reception of my message or closed even a single door. In fact, I believe they opened doors that might otherwise have remained shut. The deeper truth was that my underlying belief in the absolutely unlimited justice and love of God enabled me to speak with a far more courageous faith than I could ever have managed without it. I am convinced that without this conviction I would have been deprived of half my power.

Whatever others may think, the revolution this discovery worked in my own experience was immense — beyond words. The spiritual romance of my life became more captivating than ever.

Every day brought some deeper and more radiant insight into the unimaginable goodness and unselfishness of God. I felt at last that I was beginning to enter into the meaning of the Apostle’s prayer for the Ephesians: that we might comprehend, with all the saints, the breadth and length and depth and height of Christ’s love, and know— even if only faintly — the love that surpasses knowledge.

Such love truly does surpass knowledge; it could arise only from the heart of a wholly unselfish God. I stood in awe before its breadth and length and depth and height, and I marveled — endlessly — that I could ever have imagined a Divine love with boundaries.

For a long time the joy of it all was so wonderful that I thought there could be nothing more to discover about God — that I had reached the final revelation.

But a further unveiling awaited me, and the fourth epoch of my soul’s life— its most entrancing chapter yet — was about to begin.

I had to endure a fair amount of what might be called persecution, though in truth I took a certain satisfaction in it, for I felt it was a grand thing to know so much more of God than those who opposed me. I often compared my feelings to those of a civilized traveler trying to explain the marvels of his world to people in a remote, “savage” country— people who could neither understand nor believe what he described. His sense of superior knowledge would make their disapproval and opposition only a reason to pity their ignorance and to bear with it patiently. On that same principle, I almost enjoyed being regarded as a heretic, and I never wanted anyone’s endorsement. To be endorsed felt, to me, like being bound; and I preferred to be a free lance, unhindered in my absolute mental and spiritual freedom. At that time the discovery I had made was not as widely known as it is now, and it seemed likely that holding what many considered a grave heresy might hinder my Christian work. And perhaps it did in some circles. But as I always had far more invitations to speak than I could possibly accept, I never truly suffered any difficulty. I tried to be courteous enough not to place on others — especially those who found my views abhorrent — the burden of endorsing me. Still, the revelation I had received was too glorious to withhold whenever a door opened. And since I refused to sail under false colors, and insisted that any place I spoke should know beforehand exactly what a “heretic” I was, I generally enjoyed all the freedom I desired. In fact, these very views — and my open confession of them under rather trying circumstances — opened the way for some of our most important and fruitful work. It happened in this way. In 1873, my husband came to England to hold meetings in the interests of the Higher Life, or what I prefer to call the Life of Faith. I followed soon after, and upon my arrival in London I was invited to meet a gathering of leading Evangelical ladies who were to decide whether it would be safe for them to support me and lend their influence to the work. I shall never forget my first sight of Hannah Smith. We called her the ‘angel of the Churches,’ and she looked like one, with her golden hair and clear, beautifully cut face, in a dress all her own, yet as simple as that of the Friends among whom she had been raised. “What especially drew me to her that day was this. I must confess that I was only a seeker after truth. Hannah was sitting in a small circle of excellent orthodox friends, gathered to hear the good things she had to share, and she was, in fact, on trial. She had seen a funeral procession in the street, and when she mentioned it, we all adopted the conventional expression of sorrow. ‘Oh,’ she said, ‘when I see a funeral I always give thanks for a brother or sister delivered from the trials and pains of this mortal state.’ I thought, How wonderful! And I could not help asking, ‘Is that possible? Do you feel this about everyone?’ I was indeed an enfant terrible. “She paused for a moment and glanced around. She was among evangelicals, at a time when the universal hope was considered a heresy, and this was her examination. She later said she experienced a brief inner struggle. But truth prevailed, and with her bright, fearless look she said, ‘Yes— about everyone. I knew I was being tested, and I suspected that my answer might shock the entire company. Thee need not think I would be troubled at not being allowed to speak in the meetings, for nothing would suit me better. I am not in the least anxious to preach. Indeed, I consider it quite a favor on my part to be willing to do it at all, and just as much of a favor on others’ part to listen to me. If your committee should say, ‘We do not want to hear you speak at Brighton,’ I would have thanked them heartily. No one need feel any delicacy about this. fields.title: The Fourth Epoch In My Religious Life (the Life Of Faith)
fields.body_html:
It was in 1865 that the fourth, and by far the most captivating, epoch of my spiritual journey dawned upon my soul. I had been a Christian for nine years — years filled with delight and enchantment — but what now came to me was so far beyond all that preceded it that it felt as though an entirely new and magical world had opened before me.

During those earlier years, my faith had been thoroughly satisfying in everything relating to God.

Every discovery I made about His character and His ways brought me only joy. But when it came to my own part in the Christian life, the satisfaction was far less complete. I was happy, yes, but I was not the person I longed to be.

I had found a religion that promised perfect deliverance for the future, but it did not seem to offer deliverance now . I had found an unselfish and just God whom I could worship without fear of disappointment — but I was continually disappointed in myself. I knew I was not what I ought to be. My life felt full of failure — not so much outward sin, but inward sins: coldness, spiritual deadness, lack of Christian love, roots of bitterness, all those hidden failings over which God’s children so often grieve. When I wanted to do good, evil was present. The good I desired, I did not do; and the evil I despised, I still did. I found myself constantly sinning and repenting, making resolutions and breaking them, hating what was wrong yet yielding to it, longing for victory but more often failing than overcoming.

Yet Scripture seemed to teach that Christ came to bring a real and present victory to His followers. It implied that Christians were meant to be free from anxious cares and fears, and to enjoy even now a peace that surpasses understanding. But I knew painfully little of that. My heart was at rest about my future , but my present was torn by a thousand daily worries and anxieties. The very fruits of the Spirit — which I believed I had received — were love, joy, peace, patience, gentleness, meekness, goodness; yet these were the very qualities in which I felt most deficient.

This was not what I had expected when I first became a Christian. Raised among the Quakers — whose lives radiated peace — and taught from childhood that goodness was essential, I had assumed that becoming a Christian necessarily meant becoming peaceful and good. I expected victory over sin and over worry as naturally as I expected the sun to rise. But in the secret depths of my soul, I had to admit that I was disappointed.

At first, the joy of my newfound salvation had swept everything else aside. I thought temptation and fear and sin were gone forever. But when the initial glow faded, the old temptations returned with their old power. It became as easy as ever to be anxious, worried, burdened, irritable, unkind, critical, and severe — to do and be all the things from which I believed religion would deliver me. None of this ever shook my conviction that I was God’s child and an heir of heaven, but it often made me feel miserably ashamed. To be a child of God and yet unable to live like one made me wonder whether I had missed something in the Christian life — something that could have brought me victory.

Determined to discover what that missing element was, I questioned several older Christians. But they all gave me the same answer: No, you have not missed anything. The life of sinning and repenting is all we can expect in this world, because of the weakness of the flesh. They explained that the old Adam, inherited at birth, and the new Adam, received at conversion, constantly warred against each other — sometimes one prevailing, sometimes the other — and that only in death would we find true deliverance from the old nature.

Nothing could have described my condition better than Paul’s own lament in Romans 7:14– 23. It seemed written for me. Again and again I cried out with him, “O wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” But I could not understand why Paul even asked that question if, as everyone said, there was no deliverance in this life. Surely he knew the old nature was destined to remain until death. Yet he not only asked the question — he answered it triumphantly: “I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

What could he have meant? I had entered into salvation through Jesus Christ, yet I knew nothing of such triumphant deliverance. I was still bound by the “body of death” within me.

Why? Where lay the difficulty?

These questions grew even more pressing after I discovered the unlimited love of God. It felt so ungenerous — almost ungrateful — to respond to His boundless unselfishness with such lack of spiritual fruit. Since He had shown Himself so mighty to save in the future, how could He be powerless in the present?

The Quaker lives around me also suggested there must be deliverance, for they claimed to have experienced it — even though they could never explain clearly what it was or how it worked.

Another influence strengthened this conviction. I owned a book that taught not only that God’s children were commanded to bear the fruits of the Spirit, but that they could do so — and that also offered hints of the mystical pathway toward it. The book was Spiritual Progress , a collection of selections from Fenelon and Madame Guyon. It was especially precious because it had been a gift from my adored father and always lay on my desk beside my Bible.

My father had discovered it when he was only eighteen. As he walked through Philadelphia on his way to board a ship for a long voyage to China, he passed a second-hand bookstall. Though he had only recently begun the spiritual life, he was drawn to the title Spiritual Progress .

Knowing nothing of its contents, he bought it on impulse — guided unconsciously, no doubt, by the Lord in whom he had begun to trust. He wrote in his Reminiscences: “This book proved to be of the greatest comfort to me. I carried it in my pocket and read it in spare moments, to my everlasting profit, I trust. I cannot but thank a kind Providence for placing this blessed book in my hands.”

My father valued that book so highly that as soon as each of us children was old enough, he gave us our own copy and asked us to study it carefully. Because we loved him so dearly, we always wanted to please him, and during the years of my first hungry and despairing search for God, the book became my constant companion.

But since it was written more to guide souls who were already progressing in the spiritual life than to help seekers enter that life in the first place, it wasn’t of much definite help to me during those early, blind years of searching. And when, in 1858, I came to believe I had discovered “the plan of salvation”— settled, as I imagined, in the councils of Heaven, revealed in the life and death of Christ, and neatly formulated by the Apostle Paul — I filled the margins of my copy with what I thought were decisive critiques proving the book’s unsoundness.

Still, without my realizing it, its teachings made a profound impression on me. Even while I criticized it, I felt an underlying hunger for the mystical side of religion that the book expressed.

Throughout the years that followed, I was pulled back and forth between the claims of Plymouth Brethren doctrine on one side and the claims of mysticism on the other.

The practical, businesslike part of my nature leaned toward the Brethren; my Quaker upbringing and the influence of my cherished book pulled me toward the mystical.

At times, doctrines seemed supremely important and one’s actual life almost insignificant; at other times, doctrines felt worthless unless they resulted in a righteous life. Sometimes Paul held sway in my thinking — teaching salvation by faith — and sometimes James, insisting that faith without works is dead. My Plymouth Brethren friends exalted Paul and justification by faith; my Quaker friends and the Catholic saints in my book exalted James and justification by works. The practical part of me leaned to the first; the mystical side leaned to the second. The result was an ongoing restlessness of soul which, combined with my distress over my continual spiritual failures, often made me question whether what I had learned about the salvation of Christ could really be the whole story.

With no better remedy, I turned increasingly to “sound doctrine” to quiet my unrest. Under Plymouth Brethren influence, these doctrines had become very clearly defined, each one neatly labeled and stored away in the mental pigeonholes of my mind. Nothing could have been more orderly — at least as far as doctrines were concerned. I had become quite a successful teacher of these doctrines, and I looked down pityingly on anyone who was not as clear and definite as I was.

I often wished I could seat all the religious teachers I knew in a row of baby high chairs before me, so that I could explain to them the doctrines they seemed so confused about — especially justification by faith and the judicial standing of the believer . I regularly declared that if one simply understood these two points and believed them fully, then everything was all right and nothing else mattered much.

I remember saying something like this to a cousin who came to me distressed about her shortcomings in the Christian life. She said, “But Hannah, according to what you’re saying, all our sins — past, present, and future — are forgiven if we simply believe. It makes very little difference what we do.”

“Yes,” I answered in my ignorance, “and that is exactly the beauty of it! We wear the robe of Christ’s righteousness, and that robe covers all the vileness underneath. When God looks at us, He sees not our unrighteousness but Christ’s righteousness, and He accepts us because of that.”

Another time, a Quaker preacher who had heard me expound these crude ideas said, “ It seems to me, Hannah Smith, that you talk as if you could walk into a ready-made clothing shop, buy garments of salvation, put them on immediately, and come out fully clothed in righteousness and ready for heaven.”

“Yes!” I replied. “That is exactly how it is —except I don’t have to buy the garments; Christ gives them to me! Thank you for such a beautiful illustration; I shall certainly use it in my preaching.”

I have no doubt I interpreted Plymouth Brethren teaching in a far more literal and external way than they ever intended. But I liked to have everything defined with absolute clarity, and this seemed the logical outcome of their views. Strangely, I failed to see how inconsistent it was to believe in a righteous God who supposedly covered up our unrighteousness with the robe of His own righteousness, and then pretended to Himself that we were fit for heaven — when He certainly knew that beneath the robe our “filthy garments” were still there.

Whenever my Quaker friends hinted at this inconsistency, I silenced my uneasiness by telling myself that although they were dear, good people, they were not doctrinal at all and knew very little about the “plan of salvation,” “justification by faith,” or the “judicial standing of the believer.” Their objections, therefore, were not worth considering.

However, after the discovery I had made of the vastness of God’s love , as described in my previous chapters, I began to feel increasingly uneasy. It seemed a most ungrateful response to such boundless love that we — its recipients — should fail so miserably in living the kind of life God clearly intended for us. The more I thought, the more inconsistent it seemed that salvation, which was ultimately to be so magnificent and complete, should fail so obviously now , in this present life, to provide the victory over sin and over worry that the gospel so plainly promises as its immediate result.

Why was it, I asked myself again and again, that the God who had planned such a glorious deliverance for us in the future had not also planned a better deliverance for us in the present?

fields.title: The Way Of Escape
fields.body_html:
This unrest and questioning came to a head in 1865. Because of family circumstances, we had to leave our delightful home in Germantown — along with all our wide circle of interests — and move to a remote village in New Jersey, where we were almost completely cut off from any congenial society. Financially, it was an advantage, but in every other respect it was a tremendous trial, especially for me. I confess that my spirit rebelled bitterly against the change.

Little did I imagine that in this very place, which felt so desolate and isolated, a glorious new light would dawn, ushering in the fourth and crowning epoch of my spiritual life.

It happened this way. As I’ve said, I was deeply rebellious about the move. Yet I had enough spiritual insight to know that this rebellion was wrong. I have grown much in knowledge, but not in grace, and I find that I have no more real power over sin than I did when I was first converted. This has not led me to doubt that I am a child of God — justified, forgiven, possessing eternal life, and heir to a heavenly inheritance.

But even with this assurance, I cannot be happy while my heart condemns me. I long for more holiness, more power over sin, more unbroken communion with God. But I do not know how to attain it. Resolutions are useless; my efforts in vain. My prayers go unanswered. A thousand times I have been ready to give up in despair and conclude that it is not God’s will for me ever to gain victory over sin. And yet the Bible presents such a different picture —‘blameless, harmless, without rebuke’; with every temptation a ‘way of escape’; ‘purified’; ‘conformed to the image of Christ’; ‘holy as He is holy.’”

Then I wrote: “I find there are Christians who say that by receiving Christ by faith for our sanctification, just as we received Him by faith for our justification, all this work I long for is accomplished — that is, the method of accomplishing it is discovered. They claim that the Bible teaches that the Lord can deliver from the power of sin as well as from its guilt, and that the soul learns to trust Him to do this, ceasing to rely on its own resolutions or efforts at holiness, and committing the entire work of being kept from evil to the Lord alone.”

And finally: “I am beginning to see more clearly that the Lord is worthy of the most unlimited and boundless confidence; and perhaps this is the first dawning of the light I have been seeking. It is a Methodist doctrine, and I have long been accustomed to hearing Methodists criticized for it, but it seems to be the only thing that meets my need, and I feel compelled to try it.”

On February 11, 1867, I recorded my early efforts to grasp this conquering faith, and wrote: “My soul’s present posture is one of trusting the Lord. And I’ve discovered that this is a practical reality — He actually does deliver. When temptation comes, if I turn to Him at once with the prayer, ‘Lord, save me. I cannot save myself from this sin, but You can and will,’ He never fails.

Either He completely changes my feelings or He makes me forget the whole matter — and the victory, or rather His victory, is complete. This is a secret of the Christian life I never knew before.

But why did I not know it? Why has my path been so halting and miserable when I might have lived in victory? I am a striking example of the inherent legalism and unbelief of the human heart. While trusting the Lord entirely for my justification, I have always trusted myself for my sanctification.

I have relied on my own efforts, resolutions, watchfulness, fervor, and striving to accomplish holy living. This was legalism — just as truly legalism as if I had trusted these things to save my soul in the first place. I was ‘frustrating’ the grace of God as fully in sanctification as those whom I had condemned as legalists were frustrating it in justification. I could easily see how they nullified Christ’s death by their legal efforts, but I was blind to the fact that I was doing the same thing. Their striving and mine differed in the goal, but in both cases it was self and not Christ. For ‘if righteousness comes by the law, then Christ died in vain.’

But now how different everything is! Now I entrust my daily life to Him just as I entrust my eternal destiny. I trust Him just as nakedly in one as in the other. I am equally powerless in both.

I can do nothing —not even I, the ‘new man’— and if the Lord does not do everything, nothing will be done.

And oh, glorious truth — He does do it! When I trust Him, He gives deliverance from the power of sin as well as from its guilt. I can place everything in His care — my troubles, my temptations, my growth, my service, my daily life, moment by moment. Oh, the rest and calm of living this way!

And this is the Methodist ‘blessing of holiness.’ Expressed by them in terms I do not fully endorse, and surrounded by what seems to me a mixture of error — but still genuinely experienced and enjoyed by them. I am truly grateful for their testimony to its reality. And I now see that it is far better to have the experience — even if mixed with error — than to live without it and be doctrinally correct, as I formerly was.”

My diary from this period is full of the astonishing discoveries I was making, but these extracts are enough. From then on, the possibilities of faith opened before me in ways I had never dreamed. I saw that faith was truly the victory that overcomes the world, and I marveled at my blindness in never having understood it.

Once again, it felt as if a veil had been stripped from the Bible, and it became a new book to me: “The truth that was mine yesterday Is larger truth today; Its face has grown more divine, Its kingship fuller sway.

For truth must grow as ages roll, And God loom larger in the soul.”

One day I was at a meeting where the speaker read John 15, and the words “Without Me you can do nothing” struck me with breathtaking force. I had read and quoted these words hundreds of times — even preached on them. But now they blazed with such meaning that it seemed as though they must have been newly added to the Bible. Here was the Lord saying plainly, “Without Me you can do nothing,” and yet all the while I had been thinking I could— and must — do so much.

What meaning had I previously given the word “nothing”? I tried to recall, but there was only a blank. I had never truly noticed it.

Another day I read the passage in Matthew 6 where Jesus tells us to “take no thought for your life,” because our Heavenly Father cares for us — citing the birds of the air and the lilies of the field, and reminding us that we are of far greater value. I read the passage repeatedly in utter astonishment. Could it possibly be true? Had it really been in the Bible all these years? If so, how had I never seen it? And yet not only had I seen it — I had memorized it and recited it often. But in the only sense that matters, I had never seen it before.

Now I saw — and at that sight, my cares, worries, fears, and anxieties vanished like mist before the sun.

The same happened with all the familiar Scriptures — they were illuminated with entirely new meaning. Every page proclaimed, as if with a trumpet, the reality of a victorious Christian life lived by faith in Jesus Christ. My whole soul burned with the discovery. I could think and speak of little else. I had found something about the salvation of Christ I had never imagined — something that proved Him a far more complete Savior than I had ever conceived.

I saw that He was not only my Savior for the future but my all-sufficient Savior for the present.

My Captain to fight my battles so I need not fight them myself. My Burden-Bearer so I could roll my burdens off my weak shoulders. My Fortress from my enemies. My Shield, my Guide, my Comforter, my Shepherd. No longer did I need to protect, defend, or fight for myself. Everything was in the hands of One mighty to save — and what else could I do but trust Him?

No words can express the fullness and sufficiency I found stored up in the Lord. I could not keep such glorious news to myself. Everyone who came near me was obliged to hear my story.

One of the first I told was the cousin I had mentioned earlier — the one who had once been puzzled by my teaching that although our sins were forgiven, we must remain lifelong slaves to sin’s power. I seized the earliest opportunity to invite her for a visit, and as soon as she arrived, I exclaimed: “Oh, Carrie, I have something wonderful to tell you. We mustn’t lose a minute!”

As soon as we were alone, I poured out my discovery — that in Christ there is not only forgiveness for sin but deliverance from its power , and that we need no longer live as slaves to sin but may be more than conquerors through Him.

She listened with astonished, perplexed interest, her expression growing more amazed at every sentence. Finally she burst out: “But Hannah, what do you mean? You always told me that even though you were a child of God, you couldn’t expect deliverance from sin or from worry— that the old Adam was too strong and the new nature too weak. When I was converted, I fully expected to be delivered from sin and unrest, but when I asked you about it, you said it was impossible in this life. And I believed you!

And now you say the opposite. It’s terribly confusing—I don’t know what to think!”

I agreed it was confusing, but it had been ignorance, not malice, that had enabled me to teach such a distorted view. Now that I had discovered something far better in the gospel, all we needed to do was abandon the old error and embrace the new truth shown us.

My cousin — who all along had instinctively felt the old view could not possibly represent the best Christ had to offer — embraced the new teaching with eagerness and lived it out far more faithfully than I did.

The practical working of my discovery amazed me. I surrendered my entire rebellious spirit to the Lord and told Him I could not conquer it but believed He could conquer it for me. Then I stepped aside, so to speak, and left the battle to Him. To my indescribable joy, He removed all my rebellion and replaced it with such peaceful acceptance of His will that the life which had seemed so distasteful now appeared pleasant —even desirable. I could say “Thy will be done” with genuine gratitude.

My discovery proved itself a practical success, and I was delighted. I tested it in countless ways — and it never once failed. One instance in particular remains vivid in my mind.

There came a time when I was treated in a way I felt was utterly unfair — unjustifiable then, and still unjustifiable now when I look back on it. I felt deeply wronged and was strongly tempted to retreat into a long, simmering sulk, letting my silence and coldness express the indignation I felt so keenly.

But the moment the temptation came, I saw at once the way of escape. I hurried off to be alone, practically running to my bedroom because I was so full of provocation that I couldn’t even walk calmly. I slammed the doors behind me, desperate for privacy to fight the battle out.

Once alone, I knelt down and prayed: “Lord, I am provoked. I want to be provoked. And honestly, I think I have good reason.

But I know I shouldn’t give in to this, and I want victory. I give this whole matter to You. I cannot fight this battle —You must fight it for me. Jesus saves me now.”

I said those words while my heart still felt completely rebellious. Outwardly, it probably looked as though I was declaring a lie. I didn’t feel saved from my anger, and it didn’t seem at all likely that I could be. But by faith I clung to the truth, insisting — even in the midst of turmoil — that the Lord could and did save me now.

And then it happened.

Instantly, a calm as bright as a summer morning settled over me. All my resentment vanished.

My anger dissolved. I felt as carefree and joyful as a bird in the sunshine, delighting in the very situation that only moments before had enraged me. My faith had seized hold of a divine reality: God was able to deliver, and He did deliver the soul that trusted Him.

I realized what a remarkable truth it was that I did not need to fight my own battles at all. The Lord would fight for me, and I could simply be still. Since that day, hundreds of such battles have been fought — and won — for me by the Captain of my Salvation. The secret I learned then, of placing the battle entirely in His hands and stepping aside to let Him fight, has never once failed when I have practiced it. It has proven again and again to be a living demonstration of Christ’s words: “Be of good cheer—I have overcome the world.”

He has overcome it — not we — and He always will, if only we will surrender the matter into His hands.

Never once, when I have done this, have I been disappointed. It is gloriously true — though so few seem to realize it — that He is able to save completely those who come to God through Him , because He lives forever to intercede for them. He was able when the Epistle to the Hebrews was written, and He is just as able now, for He is not dead — He still lives to intercede for us.

I had discovered that faith is the governing law of the universe . God spoke, and it was done; and when we rely on Him, we too may speak, and it shall be done. A brilliant new light shone on the words in 1 John 5:14 – 15: “This is the confidence we have in Him: that if we ask anything according to His will, He hears us. And if we know He hears us, whatever we ask, we know we have what we asked of Him.”

I had always thought such words were merely beautiful ideals — bright dreams of the Christian life that no sensible person would expect to experience on earth. But now I saw they were not dreams at all, but straightforward statements of a divine law : the law of faith, as real and as dependable as the law of gravity, if only one understands it.

Christ tells us again and again that it will be to us according to our faith, and He declares without limitation that all things are possible to the one who believes . I had assumed this was poetic exaggeration. Now I understood: He was simply describing the laws of the spiritual kingdom — laws that anyone may test and prove. Faith connects us to the almighty power of God, making it possible for our weakness to draw freely on His strength. Its possibilities seemed endless.

“Faith, mighty faith, the promise sees And looks to that alone; Laughs at impossibilities, And cries, ‘It shall be done.’”

I wish I could say that from that moment forward I continually lived in the power of this divine law. I have not. But I can say this: every time I have deliberately chosen to lay hold of God’s strength by faith, His strength has been made perfect in my weakness, and I have been victorious. Again and again I have been able to echo the apostle’s triumphant words: “In all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us.”
