I could say “Thy will be done” with genuine gratitude. My discovery proved itself a practical success, and I was delighted. I tested it in countless ways — and it never once failed. One instance in particular remains vivid in my mind. There came a time when I was treated in a way I felt was utterly unfair — unjustifiable then, and still unjustifiable now when I look back on it. I felt deeply wronged and was strongly tempted to retreat into a long, simmering sulk, letting my silence and coldness express the indignation I felt so keenly. But the moment the temptation came, I saw at once the way of escape. I hurried off to be alone, practically running to my bedroom because I was so full of provocation that I couldn’t even walk calmly. I slammed the doors behind me, desperate for privacy to fight the battle out. Once alone, I knelt down and prayed: “Lord, I am provoked. I want to be provoked. And honestly, I think I have good reason. But I know I shouldn’t give in to this, and I want victory. I give this whole matter to You. I cannot fight this battle —You must fight it for me. Jesus saves me now.” I said those words while my heart still felt completely rebellious. Outwardly, it probably looked as though I was declaring a lie. I didn’t feel saved from my anger, and it didn’t seem at all likely that I could be. But by faith I clung to the truth, insisting — even in the midst of turmoil — that the Lord could and did save me now. And then it happened. Instantly, a calm as bright as a summer morning settled over me. All my resentment vanished. My anger dissolved. I felt as carefree and joyful as a bird in the sunshine, delighting in the very situation that only moments before had enraged me. My faith had seized hold of a divine reality: God was able to deliver, and He did deliver the soul that trusted Him. I realized what a remarkable truth it was that I did not need to fight my own battles at all. The Lord would fight for me, and I could simply be still. Since that day, hundreds of such battles have been fought — and won — for me by the Captain of my Salvation. The secret I learned then, of placing the battle entirely in His hands and stepping aside to let Him fight, has never once failed when I have practiced it. It has proven again and again to be a living demonstration of Christ’s words: “Be of good cheer—I have overcome the world.” He has overcome it — not we — and He always will, if only we will surrender the matter into His hands. Never once, when I have done this, have I been disappointed. It is gloriously true — though so few seem to realize it — that He is able to save completely those who come to God through Him , because He lives forever to intercede for them. He was able when the Epistle to the Hebrews was written, and He is just as able now, for He is not dead — He still lives to intercede for us. I had discovered that faith is the governing law of the universe . God spoke, and it was done; and when we rely on Him, we too may speak, and it shall be done. A brilliant new light shone on the words in 1 John 5:14 – 15: “This is the confidence we have in Him: that if we ask anything according to His will, He hears us. And if we know He hears us, whatever we ask, we know we have what we asked of Him.” I had always thought such words were merely beautiful ideals — bright dreams of the Christian life that no sensible person would expect to experience on earth. But now I saw they were not dreams at all, but straightforward statements of a divine law : the law of faith, as real and as dependable as the law of gravity, if only one understands it. Christ tells us again and again that it will be to us according to our faith, and He declares without limitation that all things are possible to the one who believes . I had assumed this was poetic exaggeration. Now I understood: He was simply describing the laws of the spiritual kingdom — laws that anyone may test and prove. Faith connects us to the almighty power of God, making it possible for our weakness to draw freely on His strength. Its possibilities seemed endless. “Faith, mighty faith, the promise sees And looks to that alone; Laughs at impossibilities, And cries, ‘It shall be done.’” I wish I could say that from that moment forward I continually lived in the power of this divine law. I have not. But I can say this: every time I have deliberately chosen to lay hold of God’s strength by faith, His strength has been made perfect in my weakness, and I have been victorious. Again and again I have been able to echo the apostle’s triumphant words: “In all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us.”

fields.title: A Discovery, Not An Attainment
fields.body_html:
Again I want once more to make this absolutely clear: what came to me was a discovery , not an attainment . I did not suddenly become a better woman. I simply realized that Christ was a far better Savior than I had ever imagined. I was no more capable of conquering my temptations than before — but I had discovered that He was able, and that He was willing, to conquer them for me. I had no more wisdom or righteousness of my own, but I had finally learned that He could truly become for me — just as the Apostle declared — wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption .

I will never forget the first time I discovered that this was not merely a beautiful saying, but an actual, practical fact.

Not long after I first began to grasp the fullness of Christ’s salvation, I learned that someone particularly antagonistic toward me was coming to stay at our house for two weeks. She had always been provoking and difficult. As the time drew near, I felt certain that if I were to treat her in a Christlike manner, I would need far more patience than I normally possessed.

Still being new in the life of faith, I assumed the only way to obtain enough patience was to wrestle for it in prayer . My days were too busy, so I decided to devote an entire night to this spiritual struggle. After the family went to bed, I shut myself in my room, brought along a plate of biscuits in case I grew hungry, and knelt by my bed prepared for an all-night battle. I felt almost heroic, for long hours in prayer had always exhausted me; but since I desperately needed a storehouse of patience, I thought this was the only way to secure it. I expected something like a large “lump” of patience to be deposited into my heart— a reserve from which I could break off pieces whenever needed.

But no sooner had my knees touched the floor than the familiar Scripture flashed into my mind: “But of Him are ye in Christ Jesus , who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption… that he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord.”

“Yes!” I cried inwardly. “And that must surely include patience as well!”

Immediately I rose from my knees with absolute confidence that I did not need to acquire a stockpile of patience ahead of time. Instead, I could simply look to the Lord for a present supply whenever the need arose. I saw Christ as a vast, inexhaustible storehouse, always open, always full — offering exactly the grace required at exactly the moment it was required. And suddenly it seemed absurd for me to carry about packages of grace in my spiritual pockets, which — even if I could gather them — would be misplaced the very moment I needed them most.

Naturally, that faith was fully answered. My visitor proved even more aggravating than usual, yet patience came to me moment by moment — always exactly enough for the moment at hand.

Even more wonderful than the patience itself was the discovery I had made: the storehouse of God’s grace is always open , and His supplies are always available to His children.

Some people might call my patience an “attainment.” But I had not attained anything. I had simply discovered God’s supply and taken hold of it by faith, hour by hour, as each hour required.

When reduced to its simplest form, my discovery was this: In Christ there is a perfect supply for every need, and faith alone is the channel through which that supply flows. Struggling cannot bring it. Wrestling cannot bring it. Worrying and agonizing cannot bring it. Faith always will. Faith always does.

It seems such a simple realization — one would think that any believer who reads the Bible would immediately know it. But I did not know it, not even after nine years of careful study and earnest striving. And when at last I discovered it, it revolutionized my life.

There was nothing mysterious about it. It wasn’t something added to the gospel— it was the true meaning of the gospel. Christ came, according to Scripture, to accomplish certain things; my discovery was simply that He could actually be depended on to accomplish them . And if that is true, then surely those who desire these things accomplished should hand them over to the One who has undertaken the work.

To me, this seemed — and still seems — not some extraordinary spiritual attainment, but simple, practical common sense . When I hire a builder to construct a house, it is because he knows how to build and I do not. I don’t consider handing the job to him to be some great “attainment” on my part — it is merely sensible. If I come to a roaring river and find a bridge, I do not consider crossing it an accomplishment — I merely take advantage of what has been provided.

For this reason, I much prefer the word gifts to attainments . Attainments imply my own work and effort; but Christian graces are free gifts from God. Those who “reign in life” are not those who rise to great heights by their own efforts, but those who receive abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness. If God did not spare His own Son, but gave Him up for us all, how shall He not with Him freely give us all things?

To discover that all things are truly ours is not an attainment — it is a magnificent discovery. And any soul that discovers such riches would be profoundly lacking in common sense not to take possession of whatever it needs.

No angel could fully describe what this discovery meant to me. But it is enough to say that life was transformed. Where defeat and failure once ruled, victory and triumph became my daily and hourly experience — whenever I chose to take hold of them by faith. I was no longer a slave to sin, forced to obey it even when I hated it, but had entered into the liberty Christ gives, no longer bound by the old chains.

I had thought myself happy before, but now my joy was beyond words. At times it seemed to me that even Heaven itself could scarcely offer more. Yet this joy was not rooted in myself, nor in any achievement of my own — for I had none. It was joy in the Lord.

I understood, at last, t he prophet’s words: “Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the mighty man in his might, nor the rich man in his riches; but let him who glories, glory in this: that he understands and knows Me.”

I had no wisdom, no strength, no riches in myself — but I was learning to know the Lord, and in Him I could glory with all my heart.

“Where, then, is boasting?” asks the Apostle.

“It is excluded… by the law of faith.”

A soul that has no attainments cannot boast in itself; and a soul that receives everything freely from the Lord cannot help but boast in Him.

“For by grace you are saved through faith… not of yourselves… not of works, lest any man should boast.”

“They did not gain the land by their own sword, nor did their own arm save them; but Your right hand, O Lord, and the light of Your countenance.”

This was my experience. And with all my heart I could echo the Psalmist: “In God we boast all day long, and praise His Name forever.”

fields.title: The Secret Of A Happy Life
fields.body_html:
This new spiritual life I had entered had been given many different names. The Methodists called it “the Second Blessing” or “the Blessing of Sanctification.” The Presbyteri ans preferred “the Higher Life” or “the Life of Faith.” The Friends spoke of it as “the life hidden with Christ in God.” Whatever the terminology, the truth behind each phrase was exactly the same, and it could be reduced to four simple words: “Not I, but Christ.”

In every case, the heart of the matter was surrender — turning ourselves over to the Lord so that He might work within us, shaping both our desires and our actions according to His will. It meant taking Him at His word: trusting Him not only to save us from sin’s punishment but also from sin’s power, and believing His promise to give us grace and help in every moment of need.

Personally, I prefer to call this simply “the life of faith,” because that is the plainest description.

But in the book where I explained it most fully, I called it The Secret of a Happy Life , because for so long it truly had been a secret to me — and because I fear it is still a secret to hundreds of God’s children who are staggering under the same heavy burdens I once carried. It was not a secret because God hid it, but because I had not yet discovered it. It has always been an open secret — spread clearly across the pages of Scripture — if only I had possessed the spiritual perception to see it.

“The secrets of the gods are from of old, Guarded forever, and forever told; Blabbed in all ears, but published in a tongue Whose purport the gods only can unfold.”

An ox and a philosopher may look at the same field, yet see entirely different things. In the same way, before and after this glorious discovery, I looked at the same Bible and even read the same verses — but I saw them with entirely different eyes. Scripture, like nature, lies open to all, but not all truly see it. The law of gravitation operated plainly before humankind for ages, but only Newton recognized it. Likewise, the law of faith had been written plainly in the Bible, though I had failed to discern it. The forces we harness in nature were not created by us, only discovered; they existed just as truly before discovery as afterward. And I am certain that no scientific discoverer ever felt greater delight in uncovering nature’s secrets than I felt when I uncovered the “secrets of God.”

My joy was so great that I felt compelled to speak of it to everyone — to insist upon their listening. At first, my husband — an earnest and successful Christian worker — was somewhat alarmed. He feared I might be rejoicing in some error that would harm me and perhaps others.

He frequently returned to the argument that the “old man” within us could never be completely conquered in this life, and must always hold us in some degree of bondage.

One morning, as we were discussing this, I said, “Well, impossible or not, the Bible certainly says it. What does thee make of this passage in Romans 6: ‘Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with Him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin.’ What else can that mean but that sin’s power is truly to be conquered, so that we need no longer serve it?”

Startled by the sudden light that seemed to flash from those words, he said, “There is no such passage in the Bible.”

“Oh yes, there is,” I replied. I opened my Bible and showed it to him. It was a verse he had, of course, known for years, yet in that moment it appeared to him with such a new and striking meaning that he felt as if he had never seen it before. It brought with it a deep conviction, and from that moment he did not rest until he had discovered the truth for himself.

His own account of this discovery, published in 1868, was as follows. After describing the lack he had been feeling in his Christian life, he continued: “I knew that the Bible seemed to promise a better life for the Christian than the one I knew, and for years the conviction had grown in me that there was some part of God’s truth that I had yet to discover. I felt that something essential was missing in the way I understood Scripture — something that would supply that spirit of love which the Bible declares is greater than all knowledge and all faith. I had often expressed my growing sense that some truth was waiting to break forth from God’s Word— something that would fill our hearts with a love that could bear all things. My feeling was so strong that I arranged a meeting with several brethren well-versed in Scripture so that we might examine, carefully and in detail, what part of God’s Word we had failed to understand and to teach.

Circumstances delayed that meeting, but in the meantime — through a completely unexpected channel — I received the secret that taught me the joy of Christian liberty and the power of true service. That secret was faith . How strange that I, who had constantly taught faith as the channel for the forgiveness of sins, had failed to see that faith alone is also the means of deliverance from the inward power of sin. Not only the sinner, but the Christian also, must receive everything by faith.

“At this time, I met some Christians whose inner life, as they described it, seemed utterly different from mine. They declared that practical sanctification was obtained, just like justification, by simple faith; that it could be realized at any moment when one’s faith could fully grasp it; and they insisted that they themselves had experienced it. The subject continued to confront me, and again and again passages of Scripture were presented to me — passages to which I sincerely believed myself completely submissive. Yet I regarded the entire matter with profound unease, for it seemed to me that what they sought and claimed to possess was nothing less than perfection in the flesh —and that, I knew, was impossible.”

I can hardly describe the depth of prejudice I felt against this teaching. Few ideas had ever stirred such instinctive resistance in me, and I spent many anxious hours worrying over what I believed were the dangerous consequences of this “heresy” creeping in among us. My opposition was so determined that even familiar passages of Scripture — texts I had known for years — seemed strange and almost unrecognizable when someone quoted them to prove that sanctification was by faith, and that it was possible to “walk worthy of the Lord unto all pleasing.”

One morning, Romans 6:6 was read to me: “Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with Christ, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin.” My friend added, “Surely these words must mean something — and something that makes it possible for a believer to cease being a slave to sin.”

I was so startled by the force of the verse that I blurted out emphatically, “That passage is not in the Bible!”— even though, in truth, it was one of the most familiar passages in all of Scripture to me. When I was forced to admit that it really was there, I took refuge in the explanation that it was merely judicial truth: something true “in God’s sight,” but never actually true in a Christian’s experience.

But from that moment, I began to wonder whether there might be some truth in what these people were teaching. Slowly it dawned on me that I had misunderstood them. They were not talking about perfection in the flesh, but about the death of the flesh — and a life hidden in Christ.

A life of abiding in Him, walking in Him, living through His power — a life of victory and joy that was truly pleasing to God.

“So that is all you mean?” I asked once, when this truth had been pressed upon me with unusual force. “That is nothing new. I have always known that.”

“But have you lived it?” came the reply.

“Yes,” I answered, “I have lived so at times. Often I have given myself wholly into the Lord’s care and realized that I was dead, and that He alone lived in me.”

“You have known this as an occasional experience,” my friend said gently. “But have you ever known it as a life ? You say you sometimes take refuge in the Lord — but have you ever made your home in Him?”

I saw at once that I had not. My faith in this matter had been intermittent. In moments of unusual difficulty, or whenever I felt especially weak, I had turned exclusively to the Lord and had always found Him sufficient for my need. But that this occasional experience might become — and ought to become — the experience of my whole life had never occurred to me.

“What would you think,” my friend continued, “of people who trusted Christ in such an intermittent way for the salvation of their souls? Suppose one week they felt powerless and cast themselves entirely on Him, only to spend the next week trying to earn salvation partly themselves, merely asking Him to make up what they lacked. Would you not think such a course inconsistent and foolish? And yet is it not just as inconsistent — and just as dishonoring to Christ — to trust Him in this on-again, off-again way for your daily life? Sometimes walking by faith, sometimes relying on your own strength?”

I could not deny the truth of this, and the possibility — and beauty — of a life of continuous faith began to open before me.

Such was my husband’s account of his discovery. To my great joy, from that time forward we were entirely united in the matter. It was not that either of us believed we had become sinless, or that we never failed again. Rather, we had discovered the secret of victory — that we were no longer slaves to sin, compelled to yield to its power, but could, if we chose, become “more than conquerors through Him who loved us.”

This did not mean temptations ever ceased. But we had learned that the Lord is both able and willing to deliver us out of every temptation — if only we would trust Him. We saw that our old belief —that we were doomed to be lifelong “servants of sin”— was contrary to Scripture and a slander upon the completeness of Christ’s salvation, for He died precisely to free us from sin’s bondage. “For sin shall not have dominion over you, for you are not under the law, but under grace.”

We learned further that faith — faith alone — was the road to victory, and that effort and self-struggle accomplished nothing in this battle. Our part was surrender and trust; God’s part was everything else.

For the third time, as I have said, a veil seemed to lift from the pages of Scripture, and everywhere we saw the “secret of victory” shining in letters of light. Old texts blossomed with new fullness. Take, for instance: “For whatsoever is born of God overcomes the world; and this is the victory that overcomes the world, even our faith. Who is he that overcomes the world, but he that believes that Jesus is the Son of God?” Formerly we thought this referred only to a future victory, after death. Now we saw it spoke of a present victory, by a present faith, while still living in the world.

Or this: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.” We had always taken it to mean the removal of sin’s penalty . Now we saw it meant the removal of its power — that we need no longer serve it or be enslaved by it.

I could give countless examples of this unveiling of Scripture, but these must suffice. We had made a transforming discovery, and it filled our every thought. Whenever I met a friend, my first question was, “How much time do you have? I have something wonderful to tell you.” And I would pour out my story of the great salvation I had discovered.

To most, it was as new and delightful as it had been to me, and many immediately embraced it as an experiential reality. But one friend — the same who had awakened me to religious things at sixteen, and who had been my closest spiritual confidante ever since — listened and then said, “But Hannah, that is nothing new. I have always known that.”

“Then why,” I cried indignantly, “did you never tell me? You knew how I have struggled all these years — winning a few battles, losing far more — and all the while you had this secret of victory and never told me! How could you be so unkind?”

“But I thought everyone knew it,” she said. “It is what the Quakers have always taught. Their preaching is almost entirely about it.”

“Well,” I said, “everyone does not know it. Very few know it. Most Christians believe they must remain ‘servants of sin’ all their lives because of the weakness of the flesh. And most think that if they are ever to gain victory, they must fight for it themselves, and only if defeat seems imminent may they call the Lord to help. They do not understand that the battle is to be handed over to Him from the beginning — just as the Israelites stood still at the Red Sea and saw the salvation of the Lord.”

“And,” I added with conviction, “I intend to tell this to everyone I can.”

And I did. Young or old, whether mature Christians or beginners — no one escaped hearing the story if I dared speak. Nearly all who heard it embraced it and began to live in its power.

One of them was my little daughter, about seven or eight years old. She had begun to develop a strong willfulness that I found almost impossible to manage. She herself recognized it as wrong and tried hard to conquer it, but she seemed almost possessed by it. One day she came to me, puzzled, and said, “Mother, why am I so naughty? I know I’m a little Christian girl, and I thought Christian children were always good. But no matter how hard I try to make myself good, I just can’t help being naughty.”

From my own experience, I understood her perfectly. I said, “I think, darling, the reason is that you are trying to make yourself good. We never can make ourselves good, try as we may. Only our Heavenly Father can do that. Whenever you feel tempted to be naughty, tell Him all about it, ask Him to make you good, and then trust Him to do it. He will surely take the naughtiness away.”

She thought a moment and said, “Oh, I didn’t know that. I thought you had to use your will and just do it yourself.”

She walked away quietly, clearly considering this new idea. Soon I noticed a great change. Her willfulness seemed entirely gone; she was gentle and obedient as a lamb. I said nothing, wanting to respect the delicacy of the moment. A few days later, I heard her playing softly with her dolls and murmuring with quiet delight, “Oh, I am so glad Heavenly Father is making me so good. It feels so nice to be good.”

Still I said nothing. But a few nights afterward, as I tucked her into bed, she burst out, “Oh, Mother, aren’t you glad Heavenly Father is making me so good? He’s going to make me a great deal gooder, but aren’t you glad He has made me as good as I am now?”

As I hugged and kissed her, rejoicing with her, she added earnestly, “Mother, do you tell everybody about this?”

I said I tried to, but she insisted, “You mustn’t only try— you must really do it every time you preach. I think lots of people are like I was — wanting to be good but not knowing how. You must tell every single person you meet.”

I have always taken that as a kind of divine call to my work.

In truth, our hearts were so full that we hardly needed encouragement. Everyone we knew heard the story eventually, and soon a great stir arose — not only in our own community, but throughout the American church and even in England. Letters poured in from all directions asking what this “new doctrine taught by the Pearsall Smiths of Millville, New Jersey” might be. Meetings and conferences sprang up that continue even to this day, many known as “meetings for the deepening of the spiritual life.”

This discovery was the beginning of a great revival in the spiritual life of the Church everywhere. It reached its height in the meetings of 1873 and 1874 on the Continent, and later at Oxford and Brighton, where thousands came to hear the message. Its effects are still felt in countless lives. Wherever I go, people tell me their whole lives were changed by what they learned there.

It was not a new religion they discovered, but the vitality of the old one. Truths they had long professed became living realities. They had called Christ their Savior; now they learned that He truly saves , and trusting Him, they found Him faithful.

There was nothing sectarian in the teaching. No one had to change creed or denomination.

Across all churches — Methodist, Quaker, Catholic, and more — there have always been those who truly understood and lived the life of faith. It lies, I believe, at the heart of every Christian creed. All that is needed is for believers to stop merely professing their faith and begin actually believing it — and they will always find it true.

The life of faith fits every creed and every denomination. The story is the same everywhere.
fields.body_text: This new spiritual life I had entered had been given many different names. The Methodists called it “the Second Blessing” or “the Blessing of Sanctification.” The Presbyteri ans preferred “the Higher Life” or “the Life of Faith.” The Friends spoke of it as “the life hidden with Christ in God.” Whatever the terminology, the truth behind each phrase was exactly the same, and it could be reduced to four simple words: “Not I, but Christ.” In every case, the heart of the matter was surrender — turning ourselves over to the Lord so that He might work within us, shaping both our desires and our actions according to His will. It meant taking Him at His word: trusting Him not only to save us from sin’s punishment but also from sin’s power, and believing His promise to give us grace and help in every moment of need. Personally, I prefer to call this simply “the life of faith,” because that is the plainest description. But in the book where I explained it most fully, I called it The Secret of a Happy Life , because for so long it truly had been a secret to me — and because I fear it is still a secret to hundreds of God’s children who are staggering under the same heavy burdens I once carried. It was not a secret because God hid it, but because I had not yet discovered it. It has always been an open secret — spread clearly across the pages of Scripture — if only I had possessed the spiritual perception to see it. “The secrets of the gods are from of old, Guarded forever, and forever told; Blabbed in all ears, but published in a tongue Whose purport the gods only can unfold.” An ox and a philosopher may look at the same field, yet see entirely different things. In the same way, before and after this glorious discovery, I looked at the same Bible and even read the same verses — but I saw them with entirely different eyes. Scripture, like nature, lies open to all, but not all truly see it. The law of gravitation operated plainly before humankind for ages, but only Newton recognized it. Likewise, the law of faith had been written plainly in the Bible, though I had failed to discern it. The forces we harness in nature were not created by us, only discovered; they existed just as truly before discovery as afterward. And I am certain that no scientific discoverer ever felt greater delight in uncovering nature’s secrets than I felt when I uncovered the “secrets of God.” My joy was so great that I felt compelled to speak of it to everyone — to insist upon their listening. At first, my husband — an earnest and successful Christian worker — was somewhat alarmed. He feared I might be rejoicing in some error that would harm me and perhaps others. He frequently returned to the argument that the “old man” within us could never be completely conquered in this life, and must always hold us in some degree of bondage. One morning, as we were discussing this, I said, “Well, impossible or not, the Bible certainly says it. What does thee make of this passage in Romans 6: ‘Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with Him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin.’ What else can that mean but that sin’s power is truly to be conquered, so that we need no longer serve it?” Startled by the sudden light that seemed to flash from those words, he said, “There is no such passage in the Bible.” “Oh yes, there is,” I replied. I opened my Bible and showed it to him. It was a verse he had, of course, known for years, yet in that moment it appeared to him with such a new and striking meaning that he felt as if he had never seen it before. It brought with it a deep conviction, and from that moment he did not rest until he had discovered the truth for himself. His own account of this discovery, published in 1868, was as follows. After describing the lack he had been feeling in his Christian life, he continued: “I knew that the Bible seemed to promise a better life for the Christian than the one I knew, and for years the conviction had grown in me that there was some part of God’s truth that I had yet to discover. I felt that something essential was missing in the way I understood Scripture — something that would supply that spirit of love which the Bible declares is greater than all knowledge and all faith. I had often expressed my growing sense that some truth was waiting to break forth from God’s Word— something that would fill our hearts with a love that could bear all things. My feeling was so strong that I arranged a meeting with several brethren well-versed in Scripture so that we might examine, carefully and in detail, what part of God’s Word we had failed to understand and to teach. Circumstances delayed that meeting, but in the meantime — through a completely unexpected channel — I received the secret that taught me the joy of Christian liberty and the power of true service. That secret was faith . How strange that I, who had constantly taught faith as the channel for the forgiveness of sins, had failed to see that faith alone is also the means of deliverance from the inward power of sin. Not only the sinner, but the Christian also, must receive everything by faith. “At this time, I met some Christians whose inner life, as they described it, seemed utterly different from mine. They declared that practical sanctification was obtained, just like justification, by simple faith; that it could be realized at any moment when one’s faith could fully grasp it; and they insisted that they themselves had experienced it. The subject continued to confront me, and again and again passages of Scripture were presented to me — passages to which I sincerely believed myself completely submissive. Yet I regarded the entire matter with profound unease, for it seemed to me that what they sought and claimed to possess was nothing less than perfection in the flesh —and that, I knew, was impossible.” I can hardly describe the depth of prejudice I felt against this teaching. Few ideas had ever stirred such instinctive resistance in me, and I spent many anxious hours worrying over what I believed were the dangerous consequences of this “heresy” creeping in among us. My opposition was so determined that even familiar passages of Scripture — texts I had known for years — seemed strange and almost unrecognizable when someone quoted them to prove that sanctification was by faith, and that it was possible to “walk worthy of the Lord unto all pleasing.” One morning, Romans 6:6 was read to me: “Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with Christ, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin.” My friend added, “Surely these words must mean something — and something that makes it possible for a believer to cease being a slave to sin.” I was so startled by the force of the verse that I blurted out emphatically, “That passage is not in the Bible!”— even though, in truth, it was one of the most familiar passages in all of Scripture to me. When I was forced to admit that it really was there, I took refuge in the explanation that it was merely judicial truth: something true “in God’s sight,” but never actually true in a Christian’s experience. But from that moment, I began to wonder whether there might be some truth in what these people were teaching. Slowly it dawned on me that I had misunderstood them. They were not talking about perfection in the flesh, but about the death of the flesh — and a life hidden in Christ. A life of abiding in Him, walking in Him, living through His power — a life of victory and joy that was truly pleasing to God. “So that is all you mean?” I asked once, when this truth had been pressed upon me with unusual force. “That is nothing new. I have always known that.” “But have you lived it?” came the reply. “Yes,” I answered, “I have lived so at times. Often I have given myself wholly into the Lord’s care and realized that I was dead, and that He alone lived in me.” “You have known this as an occasional experience,” my friend said gently. “But have you ever known it as a life ? You say you sometimes take refuge in the Lord — but have you ever made your home in Him?” I saw at once that I had not. My faith in this matter had been intermittent. In moments of unusual difficulty, or whenever I felt especially weak, I had turned exclusively to the Lord and had always found Him sufficient for my need. But that this occasional experience might become — and ought to become — the experience of my whole life had never occurred to me. “What would you think,” my friend continued, “of people who trusted Christ in such an intermittent way for the salvation of their souls? Suppose one week they felt powerless and cast themselves entirely on Him, only to spend the next week trying to earn salvation partly themselves, merely asking Him to make up what they lacked. Would you not think such a course inconsistent and foolish? And yet is it not just as inconsistent — and just as dishonoring to Christ — to trust Him in this on-again, off-again way for your daily life? Sometimes walking by faith, sometimes relying on your own strength?” I could not deny the truth of this, and the possibility — and beauty — of a life of continuous faith began to open before me. Such was my husband’s account of his discovery. To my great joy, from that time forward we were entirely united in the matter. It was not that either of us believed we had become sinless, or that we never failed again. Rather, we had discovered the secret of victory — that we were no longer slaves to sin, compelled to yield to its power, but could, if we chose, become “more than conquerors through Him who loved us.” This did not mean temptations ever ceased. But we had learned that the Lord is both able and willing to deliver us out of every temptation — if only we would trust Him. We saw that our old belief —that we were doomed to be lifelong “servants of sin”— was contrary to Scripture and a slander upon the completeness of Christ’s salvation, for He died precisely to free us from sin’s bondage. “For sin shall not have dominion over you, for you are not under the law, but under grace.” We learned further that faith — faith alone — was the road to victory, and that effort and self-struggle accomplished nothing in this battle. Our part was surrender and trust; God’s part was everything else. For the third time, as I have said, a veil seemed to lift from the pages of Scripture, and everywhere we saw the “secret of victory” shining in letters of light. Old texts blossomed with new fullness. Take, for instance: “For whatsoever is born of God overcomes the world; and this is the victory that overcomes the world, even our faith. Who is he that overcomes the world, but he that believes that Jesus is the Son of God?” Formerly we thought this referred only to a future victory, after death. Now we saw it spoke of a present victory, by a present faith, while still living in the world. Or this: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.” We had always taken it to mean the removal of sin’s penalty . Now we saw it meant the removal of its power — that we need no longer serve it or be enslaved by it. I could give countless examples of this unveiling of Scripture, but these must suffice. We had made a transforming discovery, and it filled our every thought. Whenever I met a friend, my first question was, “How much time do you have? I have something wonderful to tell you.” And I would pour out my story of the great salvation I had discovered. To most, it was as new and delightful as it had been to me, and many immediately embraced it as an experiential reality. But one friend — the same who had awakened me to religious things at sixteen, and who had been my closest spiritual confidante ever since — listened and then said, “But Hannah, that is nothing new. I have always known that.” “Then why,” I cried indignantly, “did you never tell me? You knew how I have struggled all these years — winning a few battles, losing far more — and all the while you had this secret of victory and never told me! How could you be so unkind?” “But I thought everyone knew it,” she said. “It is what the Quakers have always taught. Their preaching is almost entirely about it.” “Well,” I said, “everyone does not know it. Very few know it. Most Christians believe they must remain ‘servants of sin’ all their lives because of the weakness of the flesh. And most think that if they are ever to gain victory, they must fight for it themselves, and only if defeat seems imminent may they call the Lord to help. They do not understand that the battle is to be handed over to Him from the beginning — just as the Israelites stood still at the Red Sea and saw the salvation of the Lord.” “And,” I added with conviction, “I intend to tell this to everyone I can.” And I did. Young or old, whether mature Christians or beginners — no one escaped hearing the story if I dared speak. Nearly all who heard it embraced it and began to live in its power. One of them was my little daughter, about seven or eight years old. She had begun to develop a strong willfulness that I found almost impossible to manage. She herself recognized it as wrong and tried hard to conquer it, but she seemed almost possessed by it. One day she came to me, puzzled, and said, “Mother, why am I so naughty? I know I’m a little Christian girl, and I thought Christian children were always good. But no matter how hard I try to make myself good, I just can’t help being naughty.” From my own experience, I understood her perfectly. I said, “I think, darling, the reason is that you are trying to make yourself good. We never can make ourselves good, try as we may. Only our Heavenly Father can do that. Whenever you feel tempted to be naughty, tell Him all about it, ask Him to make you good, and then trust Him to do it. He will surely take the naughtiness away.” She thought a moment and said, “Oh, I didn’t know that. I thought you had to use your will and just do it yourself.” She walked away quietly, clearly considering this new idea. Soon I noticed a great change. Her willfulness seemed entirely gone; she was gentle and obedient as a lamb. I said nothing, wanting to respect the delicacy of the moment. A few days later, I heard her playing softly with her dolls and murmuring with quiet delight, “Oh, I am so glad Heavenly Father is making me so good. It feels so nice to be good.” Still I said nothing. But a few nights afterward, as I tucked her into bed, she burst out, “Oh, Mother, aren’t you glad Heavenly Father is making me so good? He’s going to make me a great deal gooder, but aren’t you glad He has made me as good as I am now?” As I hugged and kissed her, rejoicing with her, she added earnestly, “Mother, do you tell everybody about this?” I said I tried to, but she insisted, “You mustn’t only try— you must really do it every time you preach. I think lots of people are like I was — wanting to be good but not knowing how. You must tell every single person you meet.” I have always taken that as a kind of divine call to my work. In truth, our hearts were so full that we hardly needed encouragement. Everyone we knew heard the story eventually, and soon a great stir arose — not only in our own community, but throughout the American church and even in England. Letters poured in from all directions asking what this “new doctrine taught by the Pearsall Smiths of Millville, New Jersey” might be. Meetings and conferences sprang up that continue even to this day, many known as “meetings for the deepening of the spiritual life.” This discovery was the beginning of a great revival in the spiritual life of the Church everywhere. It reached its height in the meetings of 1873 and 1874 on the Continent, and later at Oxford and Brighton, where thousands came to hear the message. Its effects are still felt in countless lives. Wherever I go, people tell me their whole lives were changed by what they learned there. It was not a new religion they discovered, but the vitality of the old one. Truths they had long professed became living realities. They had called Christ their Savior; now they learned that He truly saves , and trusting Him, they found Him faithful. There was nothing sectarian in the teaching. No one had to change creed or denomination. Across all churches — Methodist, Quaker, Catholic, and more — there have always been those who truly understood and lived the life of faith. It lies, I believe, at the heart of every Christian creed. All that is needed is for believers to stop merely professing their faith and begin actually believing it — and they will always find it true. The life of faith fits every creed and every denomination. The story is the same everywhere.

fields.title: The Life Of Faith Quaker Doctrine
fields.body_html:
Among those especially interested in these new spiritual discoveries were the Friends. As I mentioned in the last chapter, one of them — after hearing my story — expressed surprise that any of it was new to me. She insisted it was exactly what the Quakers had always taught.

Her comment suddenly cast a new light on Quakerism, one I had never imagined.

My mother said something similar after hearing me speak one day. “But Hannah,” she asked, “why do you call this doctrine new? You’re only preaching what the old Friends always preached.”

“Yes,” I replied, “I’m beginning to see that. But they have never preached it in a way that ordinary people could grasp. Unless one already knew the secret, their words could hardly give it. Certainly I never understood it, though I listened to their preaching all my life. For my part,” I added, “I am determined to speak plainly enough that no one can fail to understand.”

But I eventually concluded that my mother and my friend were right: what we had discovered really was genuine Quaker doctrine. With my eyes newly opened, I reread their writings and listened again to their sermons. I realized that the heart of true Quakerism is this “life hid with Christ in God,” and that their central teaching was that Christ is a present and complete Savior — One who keeps His people’s feet, as He promised, and makes them more than conquerors through His strength.

I saw that a life of absolute consecration, full obedience, and simple trust was the life they had always urged upon us. I had not understood them before because they were preaching about the building of the Christian life, while I was still searching for the foundations of that life.

Alexander Knox says that the Christian faith has “foundation truths” and “superstructure truths,” both necessary to form a complete whole. The foundation and the building are different, yet perfectly harmonious. Foundation truths introduce us to the Christian life; superstructure truths teach us how to live once we are in it. Without superstructure, the foundation remains bare and unfinished; without foundations, the superstructure is unstable.

The early Friends were, from the beginning, a society devoted to building the superstructure.

Their message was directed chiefly to Christians. Their early history shows that most of them had already been serious believers within the denominations of their day, yet had not found there what fully satisfied their spiritual hunger.

One writer describes them this way: for years they had sought the Lord with deep longing, trying every teacher, every practice, every form of devotion, yet still craving something more. They wanted the inward presence and power of the Spirit — something beyond what they could gather merely from Scripture’s letter. They longed for life, for communion with Christ, for an entrance into His kingdom and His reign within. When the light of the Spirit finally broke upon them, it came with such joy and power that they never forgot it — a sense of life poured into their hearts, drawing them into divine rest and setting them apart for God’s service.

My own dear father, a genuine and wonderfully delightful Friend, lived this early Quaker experience. We had long known that he lived a life of steady trust and simple obedience. But in our more evangelical days, we thought him unclear on doctrines such as justification by faith or the believer’s legal standing before God. We often teased him that although he was certainly good, he was also rather “unsound.”

After discovering the life of faith for ourselves, however, we became convinced that this was the secret of his steadiness. At the first opportunity I asked him, “Now, Father, isn’t this the secret of your life and the source of your strength? Haven’t you always lived this way?”

I will never forget his answer.

“Why, of course it is, daughter,” he said with a joyful triumph in his voice. “I know no other way to live. And I certainly know what it is, when the enemy comes in like a flood, for the Lord to raise His standard against him and drive him off.”

It now seems clear to me that Friends were meant to be workers on the interior life — not primarily to convert sinners, but to lead believers into a deeper walk with God and a life of abiding trust. Yet in recent days it seems to me they have drifted from this calling, striving more to do foundational work than to build the superstructure. Their traditions and methods, suited for the latter, are less suited for the former. The results, unsurprisingly, do not compare with denominations whose chief aim has long been the foundation work of evangelism.

A thoughtful Friend recently said to me that they were meant to be a strong mystical society, but feared they were becoming a weak evangelical one. I could not deny the truth in his words.

If only the Friends would again proclaim with the old clarity and power that glorious message of a full and present salvation in Christ — available here and now — the blessing to thousands of hungry souls would be immeasurable.

One of their early preachers once said: “I bring you good news. Not that the day of your redemption is near, but that it has already come. Many are already blessing God that they are redeemed and delivered from corruption’s bondage, and have more joy in His service than they ever had in the world’s. Oh, the conquering faith, the overcoming life and power of the Spirit!

We cannot help but speak of these things, and exalt the perfect gift and power of Him who not only can complete His work in the heart, but delights to do so — yes, even to tread down Satan under the feet of those who trust Him.”

No matter how vague Quaker preaching had become in my time, the early Friends spoke plainly enough. Small wonder their message spread so widely. And if today’s Friends were to sound that same clear trumpet again, I believe multitudes would respond — for the children of God are as hungry now as ever to know the fullness of Christ’s salvation.

fields.title: Holiness Camp Meetings
fields.body_html:
As may be imagined, we eagerly seized every opportunity to learn more about the truths we had discovered. And though the Friends did indeed teach them, it was among the Methodists that we found the clearest light. The Methodists spoke with great certainty: they taught that the Christian life involved two distinct experiences — the first, justification; the second, sanctification. They urged believers not to rest content with justification (that is, forgiveness), but to press on to sanctification, the “second blessing,” as they called it. I would not now express the truth in quite that way, but at the time it was profoundly helpful.

Not all Methodists embraced this teaching; many considered it too extreme. Those who did were known as “Holiness Methodists,” and it was from them that we received the greatest help. They held special “Holiness Meetings” devoted to the subject, and we delighted in attending whenever possible. Most of all, we cherished their “Holiness Camp Meetings,” held in summer in secluded forests or by the sea. These gatherings —“Meetings for the Promotion of Holiness”— were in fact great open-air conferences, drawing Christians of many denominations from across the country, all intent on seeking deeper communion with God. Living in tents beneath the trees, we spent a week or more waiting upon God and sharing together the profound things of the Kingdom.

No words can capture the extraordinary power, solemnity, and yet overwhelming joy of those meetings. We were cut off from our ordinary occupations and cares, with nothing to do but yield ourselves to the spiritual influences around us and open our hearts to what we believed to be the teaching of the Holy Spirit. Such a company of earnest Christians, all intent on drawing nearer to God, created an atmosphere of spiritual intensity that was unforgettable. Testimonies of joy resounded in every meeting, songs of praise echoed through the forest, and the radiant faces of those we met made it seem as though we stood on the very threshold of Heaven. I cannot help but pity any Christian who has never known such seasons of pure delight. For me, they were the culmination of the grand spiritual romance that religion has always been, and I count them among the most entrancing experiences of my life. Even now, the sight of a camp chair or a tent beneath the trees brings back something of that supreme happiness that filled every hour of those blessed gatherings.

On one occasion, a friend of ours — unaware of the true purpose of the meetings — came to see what they were like. Arriving early in the morning, he met worshippers returning from prayer.

Struck by their radiant expressions, he asked us, “What is the matter with all these people, that their faces shine so? Nearly everyone I have seen here has a shining face; but I met a few whose faces did not shine, and I want to know the difference.” We explained that the shining faces reflected hearts at rest in the Lord, while those without such radiance had not yet discovered the blessed secret. He listened intently, then declared , “I am determined that I too will get a shining face, and I will stay here until I do.” And indeed, within days his face shone with the joy of God’s salvation.

I shall never forget my first Camp Meeting, nor the first prayer gathering I attended there. It was an early morning meeting in a tent. Having known only the small Methodist meetings at Millville, I had no conception of the emotional atmosphere into which I had stepped. I realized, too late, that I had forgotten my handkerchief — but having never shed tears in a meeting before, I thought little of it. Yet in that gathering the fountains of my being were broken open, and floods of sweet tears poured from my eyes. In desperation I lifted my dress and used the white underskirt to dry them. Ever since, I have carried at least two handkerchiefs to every meeting, though I have never again been so overwhelmed with emotion as I was then.

That morning was my first taste of the entrancing joys of spiritual emotion, and I reveled in it. As I left the tent, a Methodist “Holiness Sister,” seeing my tears, put her arm around me, shared her own experience of sanctification, and began to guide me. Under her care, I soon learned how to receive the full benefit of the meetings. Much was said about the “blessing of sanctification,” and at every gathering we were urged to come forward to the “altar”— a simple bench set apart — to seek it. I did not fully understand what this “blessing” was, but it seemed something tangible, born of complete consecration and simple faith, and it filled people with rapturous joy. My Holiness Sister soon had me going forward to the altar myself, determined to receive whatever God had to give. The thrilling testimonies I heard continually fired my enthusiasm, and I embraced every opportunity to seek the blessing. I enjoyed it immensely, for it seemed to bring me to the very edge of unknown spiritual possibilities ready at any moment to unfold.

Apart from those moments of standing, as it were, on the threshold, no special “blessing” ever came to me from my visits to the altar. I am not naturally emotional, and the overpowering feelings others described as the essence of the blessing never fell to my share. What I did receive was the grand truth taught at those meetings — that the Lord Jesus Christ is a Savior not only from the guilt of sin but also from its power. That truth became increasingly real and effective to me. But as for any blessing apart from the truth itself, I experienced nothing. In time, I came to see that the knowledge of the truth was all the blessing I needed. Much of what was called “the blessing” seemed to me simply the emotional response of emotional natures to the discovery of a magnificent truth. For me, it came with intellectual conviction and delight; for others, with emotional conviction and delight. But in both cases the truth was the same, and it was the truth — not the emotion — that set the soul free.

My husband, however, being of a more emotional nature, did at one of these Camp Meetings receive the blessing in true Methodist fashion. He returned home radiant, filled with a divine glow that touched everyone he met. He could not speak of the meeting without moving us to tears, and it was clear he had undergone a remarkable spiritual experience. He told us of a special gathering devoted to prayer for the Baptism of the Spirit. Afterwards, he withdrew alone into the woods to continue in prayer. Suddenly, from head to foot, he was shaken by what felt like a magnetic thrill of heavenly delight. Floods of glory poured through him, body and soul, with the inward assurance that this was indeed the longed-for Baptism of the Holy Spirit. The whole world seemed transformed: every leaf and blade of grass shimmered with exquisite color, heaven opened before him as a present possession, and everyone he saw appeared beautiful, for he seemed to perceive the Divine Spirit within them. This ecstasy lasted for weeks and marked the beginning of a life of extraordinary spiritual power and blessing.

I confess I was jealous that I did not receive a similar blessing, for I felt I needed it as much as he did. I renewed my efforts to obtain it, but all in vain. I never passed from the realm of conviction into the realm of emotion. My experiences remained intellectual rather than emotional. At last I became convinced that the difference lay not in God’s favor but in the differing natures of the recipients. Emotional natures received the truth with floods of delight; I received it calmly, with intellectual joy. The truth was the same, only the manner of reception differed.

Over time I observed that emotional experiences were often less solid and permanent than intellectual ones. Emotions, by their nature, fluctuate, while true convictions remain. Once a person is convinced that two and two make four, no amount of ill health or adverse weather can shake that conviction. Feelings, however, are at the mercy of countless influences. I learned, therefore, not to seek emotions but convictions. To my surprise and delight, convictions brought me a more stable and lasting joy than many of my emotional friends seemed to know. In times of stress, their emotions flagged or vanished, and they struggled to avoid despair. Some were grateful at last to return to the stable ground of conviction, which in their emotional days had seemed barren.

This lesson took me years to learn. Meanwhile, the joy and power of the glorious secret we had discovered grew ever more practical. My soul learned to rest in absolute confidence in the keeping and saving power of the Lord. Temptations did not cease, nor did we attain “sinless perfection.” Temptations arose, failures occurred. But we had discovered a way of escape— the way of faith. We learned that Christ is a Deliverer not only from the future punishment of sin but from its present power. We realized we need no longer be slaves to sin. As far as we laid hold of this deliverance by faith, so far we were delivered. We had not pocketed holiness as a permanent possession, but we had discovered the highway of holiness and learned the secret of walking in it. When we walked there, we had victory; when we strayed, we met failure. After years of wilderness wandering, we had entered the promised land, and found it true, as God said to Israel of old: “Every place the sole of your foot shall tread upon, that have I given you.” The whole land was ours; we need only go up and possess it.

We discovered that the Bible’s words were fact: “God is able to make all grace abound toward you; that you, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work.” And we proved in experience that God truly was able — if only we were willing. Christ was revealed to us not merely as our future Savior, but as our present and complete Savior, able to keep us from falling and to deliver us from all our enemies.

For me, this was the beginning of a romance before which all others paled. It was like exploring the courts of heaven itself. Each day brought fresh revelation. Words fail me. I often called it the “bird life,” for I felt like a bird set free, soaring upward into the blue of an unfathomable sky.

Once I had been a caged bird, content because I knew nothing of the freedom beyond. Now all barriers were gone, and my soul was free to comprehend with all saints the breadth, length, depth, and height of the love of Christ, which surpasses knowledge. What once seemed unfathomable now opened into an abyss of delight.

I found that God Himself was enough. Even His promises paled beside the comfort of His presence. What did it matter if I could not find a promise to fit my case? I had found the Promiser, and He was infinitely more than all His promises. As a child, when in trouble, the mere presence of my father or mother brought instant relief. They did not need to explain or promise; their presence was assurance enough. How much more true is this of our Heavenly Father, whose very name is Love. His presence is all we need. Over and over in Scripture He settles His people’s fears with the simple words, “I will be with thee.” That means all His wisdom, love, and power are engaged on our behalf.

I learned that God’s character is our resting place. His ways or promises we may misunderstand, but His goodness cannot be mistaken. If He is good, loving, wise, just, omnipotent, and omnipresent, then all must be ordered rightly for us. Appearances may deceive, but the deeper reality is secure. As George MacDonald said, we need “eyes that can see below surfaces.” Once we discover God’s utter unselfishness, those eyes are opened, and all mysteries of His dealings are answered forever.

No wonder the Psalmist rejoiced again and again in God’s goodness: “Oh, give thanks unto the Lord, for He is good.” “Oh, trust in the Lord, for He is good.” “Oh, taste and see that the Lord is good.” Surrounded by nations whose gods were cruel, selfish, and indifferent, Israel’s triumph was to declare without fear that their God was good. And I feel it is no less a triumph today, in a world that misunderstands and maligns Him, to be able to say with absolute conviction: “Come, taste and see that the Lord is good!”

fields.title: The Lovely Will Of God
fields.body_html:
With my eyes newly opened to the absolute goodness and selflessness of God, my entire attitude toward His will was transformed. In the past, I had viewed God’s will as something set against me; now I discovered it was wholly for me. I had feared it as something harsh; now I saw it as something to embrace with joy. I once thought His will was the terrible weapon of His severity, descending upon me to punish. Now I saw it as the tender instrument of His love, bringing into my life only what was kindest and best.

I realized that the will of perfect, unselfish love could only be good, and that since God possesses all knowledge and all wisdom, His will must — by its very nature — be the best thing the universe could offer. No greater bliss could come to any of us than to have that beautiful, selfless will perfectly done both in us and for us.

Sometimes hiding myself in God’s will felt like retreating into an impregnable fortress of love and protection, where no harm could reach me. At other times it felt like sinking into the softest bed of down, resting in perfect peace. I can never fully put into words all that I began to see of the loveliness, tenderness, generosity, and infinite goodness of the will of God. I truly reveled in its sweetness.

This did not mean life would be free of trials; a wise and loving will might see trials as necessary gifts of love. Nor was it essential that I perceive the divine hand in every difficulty. My common sense told me that if God is omnipresent, He must be present in my trials as well — and, being there, He must be there to help and bless.

We are not wise enough to judge whether our experiences are truly joys or sorrows, but the Lord knows. And because He loves us with limitless, unselfish love, He cannot fail — literally cannot fail — to make even the things that appear hard, or cruel, or wicked, work together for our greatest good. I say “cannot fail” because it is unimaginable that such a God could act otherwise.

It does not matter who begins the trial — whether human malice, spiritual evil, or our own foolishness. If God allows it to reach us, then by that very permission He makes the trial His own, transforming it into a chariot of love that carries our souls to blessings we never could have reached otherwise. For the Christian who dwells in the fortress of God’s will, there are no “second causes”; nothing can enter that fortress unless the Divine Keeper of it opens the door.

And when He does, it means He has adopted that thing for our eternal good.

Joseph was sold into Egypt through the wickedness of his brothers, yet God made their cruelty the very chariot that carried him to triumph. So we may be more certain of this than we are that the sun will rise tomorrow: God’s will is the loveliest thing in the universe for us— not because it always looks best, but because it cannot be anything but best, being the will of infinite love.

I found myself continually singing Faber’s beautiful hymn: “I worship Thee, sweet will of God, And all Thy ways adore; And every day I live it seems I love Thee more and more.”

One verse delighted me especially because I so often found it true in experience: “I know not what it is to doubt, My heart is always gay; I run no risks, for, come what will, Thou always hast Thy way.”

The first time I realized this in a deeply practical way was three days after the birth of my beloved baby girl — a child I had longed for with unspeakable yearning, who felt to me like the most exquisite treasure ever entrusted to human care.

My nurse had suddenly fallen ill and was forced to leave, so we had to bring in a stranger whose looks I mistrusted and whose ignorance seemed obvious. At that time trained nurses were far less common, and I felt this one was wholly unqualified. I could hardly bear to have her touch my precious child, yet I was not allowed to care for my baby myself.

It was winter, and a bright wood fire burned on the hearth of my room. On the nurse’s first evening, after settling me in bed, she sat close to the fire with my baby on her lap. Soon she fell into a deep sleep, snoring loudly, and I awoke to see my infant lying perilously near the blaze on her slanting knees, while the nurse’s head drooped dangerously above her.

My voice was weak, and I could not rouse her. I expected at any moment to see my little one roll into the fire. I could make no one hear me, and to rise from bed and cross the cold floor might have seriously harmed my health. Yet my anxiety drove me upright, and I was struggling to stand when suddenly these words flashed through my mind: “I run no risks, for, come what will, Thou always hast Thy way.”

With those words came a deep conviction that my child was utterly safe in God’s care. A profound peace settled over me. My head sank back onto my pillow and my soul sank back into the sweetness of God’s will. I saw that my baby was cradled in the arms of almighty love. I fell asleep without a trace of fear and woke to find her being tucked beside me for her feeding.

It was beyond words beautiful to have experienced such a practical revelation of the loveliness and blessedness of the will of God.

Since that first awakening, I have had many similar insights, and I have come to know — beyond even the faintest shadow of doubt — that the will of God is the most delicious, delightful reality in the universe. This is not because life always unfolds according to my preferences, nor because of any special piety in me, but simply because plain common sense tells me that the will of perfect, unselfish love could only be delightful. Heaven is heaven precisely because God’s will is done perfectly there; and earth would inevitably resemble heaven if His will were perfectly done here.

For years I had heard Christians describe consecration to God’s will as a spiritual achievement so lofty that only a few exceptionally devout souls could hope to reach it. But once I discovered the infinite unselfishness of God, I realized that consecration is not an attainment at all — it is a priceless privilege. I am convinced that if people truly understood the beauty of His will, not only the particularly devout but every soul in existence would rush to choose it gladly for every moment of their lives.

This is not a higher degree of piety; it is simply a higher degree of good common sense. If I were lost in a trackless wilderness, unable to see any way out, and an experienced guide offered to lead me to safety, would it feel difficult or sacrificial to place myself in his hands and say, “Your will be done”? And if not, how could it feel burdensome to entrust myself to my heavenly Guide and say, “Thy will be done”? It cannot— it is impossible. Surrender to God, or consecration as many call it, is the greatest privilege offered to any soul in this life. To say “Thy will be done” is one of the most delightful sentences a human being is permitted to utter.

An old writer once said that God’s will is not a burden to carry, as so many imagine, but a pillow on which to rest. I found this profoundly true. My soul sank into His will with an indescribable sweetness of peaceful content. At other times, saying “Thy will be done” felt like a magnificent cry of victory — like raising a triumphant banner before the entire universe and daring it to oppose me. So vivid was this feeling that I found myself repeating, day and night, as a victorious soldier might sing after battle: “Thy wonderful, grand Will, my God, With triumph now I make it mine; And Love shall cry a joyous Yes To every dear command of Thine.”

But I could never fully tell all that my soul discovered when I discovered the goodness and unselfishness of God. To say that He is enough is to give a complete and unshakeable answer to every doubt and question that can ever arise. My feelings may not always confirm that prayers are answered or promises fulfilled — but what of that? Behind every prayer and every promise stands God Himself — the sheer God, if I may put it so — and if He exists at all, then He must be enough.

For years I had sung the familiar words: “Thou, O Christ, art all I want; More than all in Thee I find.”

But until now, I had never understood what they truly meant. They had sounded beautiful, but only as a poetic sentiment. Now I saw that they state a fact. I had begun to discover that He really was everything I needed — and that infinitely more than all I could ask or imagine was stored up for me in Him.

In a certain sense, my search for God ended there, for I had found that He was enough. I have discovered many other beautiful and precious truths about Him since, but at that moment I had reached Himself — the real God behind all appearances — and my heart entered into its rest. I saw that nothing else ultimately mattered: not creeds, nor ceremonies, nor doctrines, nor dogmas.
